chapters.title: Preface to the Second Edition
chapters.html:
When I wrote the first edition of this book, the hardest part of product management was the same as it had always been: deciding what to build, for whom, and why, and then getting a room full of smart, busy people to build it together. That is still the hardest part. What has changed is almost everything around it.

In the space of about two years, AI went from a feature on a few roadmaps to a working layer of the product team itself. By mid-2025, 88 percent of organizations told McKinsey they were using AI in at least one business function, up from 78 percent a year earlier, and 62 percent said they were at least experimenting with AI agents.1 Product managers now have tools that draft requirements, summarize a week of customer calls before breakfast, watch dashboards overnight and flag what moved. Some of those tools are good. Some are confidently wrong. All of them change what a product manager’s day looks like.

They do not change what a product manager is for. Someone still has to own the outcome. Someone still has to sit with a nurse at the end of a twelve-hour shift and understand why the software she was given makes her job harder. Someone still has to tell the CEO that the feature the biggest customer asked for is the wrong bet, and be right about it. AI makes the work faster. It does not make the judgment optional. If anything, the judgment matters more, because a team that can build twice as fast can also build the wrong thing twice as fast.

So this edition does three things the first did not.

It covers the numbers. The first edition promised chapters on profit and loss, unit economics and portfolio management, and did not deliver them. Chapters 6 and 7 do. A product manager who cannot read a P&L is negotiating with one hand tied behind their back.

It puts AI where it belongs: inside the work. Every chapter ends its main argument with a section called How AI changes this, and Chapter 17 is devoted to building AI products and leading teams that include AI agents. I have tried to be specific about what to hand to an agent, what to keep, and how to tell the difference.

It shows the work. Most chapters open with a scene from one fictional company, Brindlepath, followed through the whole book, and most include worked examples, templates and a one-page checklist. The figures are diagrams and charts you can use in your own planning, not decoration.

I have spent most of my career in product, much of it in healthcare, where the stakes are high, the buyers are many and the regulations are real. That shows in the examples. But the book is written for product managers in any kind of software. If you can ship a product that a hospital will buy, a clinician will use and a compliance officer will sign off on, you can ship almost anything.

Robert Merrell

  1. McKinsey & Company, The State of AI in 2025: Agents, Innovation, and Transformation, survey of 1,993 participants conducted June 25 to July 29, 2025.↩︎

chapters.title: How to Use This Book
chapters.html:
The book is organized in five parts that follow the life of a product, from the first hint of a problem to a business that scales.

  • Part 1, Foundations (Chapters 1 to 3): what the job is now, how to find problems worth solving, and how to validate them before you spend real money.
  • Part 2, Strategy (Chapters 4 to 7): vision and positioning, prioritization and roadmaps, the financial side of product decisions, and managing more than one product.
  • Part 3, Building (Chapters 8 to 11): the product team, working with engineering and design, using data well, and building trust through security, privacy and compliance.
  • Part 4, Customers (Chapters 12 to 14): designing with empathy, taking a product to market, and keeping and growing customers.
  • Part 5, Growth (Chapters 15 to 18): partnerships, scaling, building AI products, and an integrated playbook that ties it all together.

You can read it front to back, or jump to the chapter that matches the problem on your desk. Each chapter stands on its own, and cross-references point you to related material.

Meet Brindlepath

Most chapters begin with a scene from Brindlepath, a fictional company that sells care-coordination software to health systems and large physician groups. Its product helps nurse navigators and care managers track patients as they move between the hospital, specialists, home health and primary care, the handoffs where things most often fall through the cracks.

Brindlepath is invented. So are its people: Maya Smith, who joins as Vice President of Product in Chapter 1; Dev Raman, the engineering lead; Lena Park, the head of design; and the customers, clinicians and executives they work with. Brindlepath, its people, its customers and every event in its story are fictional. They are not based on any real company, client, employer or person, and any resemblance to real organizations or people is coincidental. The situations are composites of challenges that are common across the software industry, written to illustrate the ideas in each chapter. Following one company through the whole book shows how the decisions connect: the problem you choose in Chapter 2 shapes the pricing you can charge in Chapter 6, which shapes the team you can afford in Chapter 8.

Features in every chapter

  • How AI changes this. What AI tools and agents can take on in that part of the work, what they cannot, and the traps to avoid.
  • Figures. Frameworks and charts you can reuse. Charts built on real-world data cite their source. Charts that use made-up numbers to teach a point are labelled illustrative.
  • Chapter checklist. A one-page summary of the questions to ask and the work to do, for when you come back to the chapter months later with a real decision to make.

Templates for the most useful artifacts, including a problem statement, a product requirements document, a launch checklist and a one-page roadmap, are collected in the Appendix.

chapters.title: The Product Leader’s Job, Now
chapters.epigraph:
“There is nothing so useless as doing efficiently that which should not be done at all.”

— Peter Drucker
chapters.html:
Monday, 7:10 a.m.

Maya Smith’s first Monday as Vice President of Product at Brindlepath started before she reached the office. On the train, she opened the overnight digest her team’s research agent had assembled: forty-one support tickets summarized into six themes, two competitor release notes, a spike in failed logins at one hospital customer, and a draft agenda for the quarterly business review with Ambermoor Health, Brindlepath’s largest account.

It was a good digest. It was also, she noticed, wrong in one important way. The agent had grouped eleven tickets under “notification fatigue” and recommended adding a setting to mute alerts. Maya read three of the tickets in full. The nurses were not tired of alerts. They were getting alerts for patients who had already been discharged to another team, because the handoff between the hospital’s care managers and the outpatient navigators did not update ownership in Brindlepath. Muting the alerts would hide the symptom and keep the disease. The real problem was that nobody owned the patient for the forty-eight hours after discharge.

That distinction, between the request and the problem underneath it, is the job. The agent did in twenty minutes what used to take a product manager most of a Monday. It could not do the part that mattered: notice that the pattern meant something different from what it looked like, and decide what to do about it.

This chapter is about that part.

What a product leader is actually for

Ask ten companies what a product manager does and you will get eleven answers. In some, the product manager writes tickets and runs standups. In others, the product manager sets strategy for a business line with its own profit and loss. The title covers both.

Underneath the variety, the role has one constant: the product leader owns the outcome. Engineering owns how the product is built. Design owns how it works for the people using it. Sales owns the deal. Product owns whether the whole thing creates value for customers and for the business, and whether the team is working on the right problem in the first place.

Owning the outcome means answering four questions continuously, not once:

  1. Is it valuable? Will the people it is for choose to use it, or buy it, over what they do today?
  2. Is it usable? Can they figure out how to get that value without a training manual?
  3. Is it feasible? Can we build and run it with the time, skills and technology we have?
  4. Is it viable? Does it work for the business: can we sell it, support it, price it profitably and stay within the law?

These four risks will be familiar to anyone who has read Marty Cagan’s work, and they remain the best short description of the job.1 This edition adds a fifth question that used to sit quietly inside viability and now deserves its own line:

  1. Is it trustworthy? Will customers, regulators and the public trust it with their data, their decisions and, in healthcare, their health? When a product includes AI, does it behave reliably, explain itself where it needs to, and fail safely?

Trust used to be a compliance checkbox at the end of a project. In a world where software makes recommendations about patients and AI writes answers that look authoritative whether or not they are right, it belongs at the start.

How the role got here

It helps to know where the job came from, because many organizations are still running an older version of it.

The feature coordinator (roughly the 1990s and early 2000s). In the era of boxed software and long release cycles, product management grew out of marketing and project management. The product manager gathered requirements from customers and sales, wrote them into a large specification, and handed it to engineering. Success meant shipping the spec on time.

The product owner (the 2000s and 2010s). Agile development broke big specifications into small increments and gave each team a backlog. The product manager became the person who prioritized that backlog and accepted the work. Delivery got faster, but in many companies the role shrank to managing tickets. Teams shipped steadily and still built things nobody used.

The outcome owner (the late 2010s onward). SaaS changed the economics. When customers pay every month and can leave any month, shipping is not success; adoption, retention and expansion are. Product managers began to be measured on outcomes: activation rates, net revenue retention, time saved for the user. Discovery, the work of finding out what to build before building it, became a core part of the job rather than a phase at the start.

The orchestrator (now). The current shift is less about what the product manager is accountable for and more about how the work gets done. A product manager now directs a team that includes AI tools and agents alongside engineers, designers and analysts. Research synthesis, first drafts of requirements, competitive monitoring, data pulls and test-case generation can all be delegated. The product manager’s leverage has grown enormously. So has the cost of pointing that leverage in the wrong direction.

Each stage absorbed the one before it. A great product leader today still needs to write a clear requirement, still needs to run a tight backlog, and still needs to be measured on outcomes. The new layer sits on top.

The four pillars of product leadership

The first edition described three pillars of SaaS product leadership. Experience since then has added a fourth.

Pillar 1: Market understanding

You cannot build for a market you do not understand. Market understanding means knowing who has the problem, how badly, what they do about it today, who else is trying to solve it, and what constraints shape the solution. In healthcare those constraints include regulation, reimbursement and clinical workflow; in fintech they include licensing and fraud; in education, procurement cycles that follow the school year. Every market has its own physics. Chapters 2 and 3 are about learning them.

Pillar 2: Financial insight

This is the pillar most product managers neglect, and the one that most separates a product manager from a product leader. Every product decision is also a financial decision: what it costs to build, what it costs to sell and support, how it changes what customers will pay and how long they stay. A product leader who can walk into a budget meeting with a clear view of unit economics gets resources. One who cannot gets opinions. Chapters 6 and 7 cover the numbers in detail.

Pillar 3: Customer-centered innovation

Innovation is not novelty. It is a better way to get a job done for a real person. Customer-centered innovation means staying close enough to users to see the problems they have stopped noticing, and having the discipline to measure whether what you shipped actually helped. In healthcare, that includes the patient who never logs into your software but whose care depends on it.

Pillar 4: Trust and responsibility

The new pillar covers security, privacy, compliance, accessibility and, increasingly, responsible AI. It is not a department’s job that product hands off; it is a property of the product that product leadership owns. A breach, a biased model or an inaccessible workflow is a product failure, not just a technical one. Chapter 11 covers trust by design, and Chapter 17 covers the specific risks of AI features.

All four pillars rest on the same foundation: owning the outcome. A product leader who is strong in three pillars and weak in one will be found out by that one.

What great looks like

Over the years I have hired, managed and worked beside a few hundred product managers. The great ones share habits that have little to do with frameworks.

They can say what problem they are solving in one sentence, without jargon. If you cannot explain the problem to a smart outsider, the team does not understand it either.

They talk to customers every week, not every quarter. Not sales calls and not escalations, though those matter too. Conversations whose only purpose is to understand how someone works.

They separate the request from the need. A customer asking for a mute button for alerts is telling you something true about their pain and something unreliable about the cure. Maya’s Monday morning is the job in miniature.

They make decisions and write them down. A decision log, with the reasoning and the evidence, is worth more than any roadmap slide. It lets the team move without waiting for the product manager, and it lets everyone learn when a decision turns out wrong.

They say no, often and kindly. Every yes is a no to something else. Great product leaders protect the team’s focus and explain the trade-off rather than hiding it.

They know their numbers. Not every metric in the dashboard: the three or four that tell them whether the product is working, and the one or two that tell them whether the business is.

They share credit and own failure. A product leader has authority over very little and influence over almost everything. Influence comes from trust, and trust comes from how you behave when things go wrong.

Where the week goes

One of the fastest ways to understand how the job is changing is to look at a product manager’s calendar. Figure 1.2 compares a typical week for a product manager at a growing SaaS company before AI tools, and the same role with AI assistants and agents handling much of the preparation and synthesis. The numbers are illustrative, based on the pattern I see in teams I work with, not on a survey.

Two things stand out. First, the time saved is real and large, mostly in research synthesis, status reporting and first drafts. Second, and more important, the time does not automatically flow to the work that matters. In teams that adopt AI tools without changing their habits, the freed hours fill with more meetings and more documents. In teams that do it well, the hours go to customer conversations, sharper decisions and coaching. That reallocation is a leadership choice, not a side effect of the tools.

Brindlepath in practice: the decision log

One of the first habits Maya introduced was a decision log: a shared document where every significant product decision was recorded with five fields: the date, the decision, the options considered, the evidence, and what would make the team revisit it.

The first entry was the one from her Monday morning. Decision: do not build a mute setting for notifications. Options: mute setting; change notification rules; fix ownership after discharge. Evidence: 11 tickets, three read in full, all caused by patients already discharged to another team. Revisit if: notification complaints continue after ownership is fixed.

Within a few months the log had changed how the company argued. When the head of sales pushed again for the mute setting, Maya did not have to win the argument from memory; she pointed to the entry and asked whether the evidence had changed. It had not. When a decision did turn out wrong, such as an early choice to show discharges from all units by default, the log made it easy to see why it had seemed right at the time and what the team had missed. Nobody was blamed. The team simply learned faster.

The log also became the best onboarding tool the company had. New product managers read the last six months of entries in their first week and understood more about the product’s history and reasoning than any slide deck could tell them. Dev Raman’s engineers began reading it too, because it told them why they were building things, not just what. Two of them started adding their own entries for technical decisions that affected the product.

The decision log is not complicated, and it is not glamorous. It is one of the cheapest ways a product leader can make the team’s judgment visible, shareable and improvable, which is, in the end, what owning the outcome requires.

Common mistakes

Acting as the team’s boss. Product managers who issue instructions to engineers and designers get compliance, not ideas. The role carries accountability for the outcome, not authority over how others do their work. Lead through clarity, evidence and trust.

Becoming the team’s secretary. The opposite failure: taking notes, chasing tickets and scheduling meetings while nobody owns the hard questions. If most of your week is coordination, you are doing a project manager’s job, and nobody is doing yours.

Confusing busy with valuable. A full calendar and a long list of shipped features feel like progress. The question is whether anything changed for customers. Review your last month: which of your hours moved an outcome?

Ignoring the business. Product managers who talk only about users and never about revenue, margin or retention end up with roadmaps the leadership team does not trust. The four pillars need each other.

Treating trust as someone else’s job. Security, privacy and accessibility failures land on the product, and on its leader, regardless of which department was supposed to catch them.

Letting tools set the agenda. New AI tools arrive every month. Adopting them without changing how you work just produces more output. Decide what you want more time for, then choose tools that create it.

Try this

Take one week of your calendar and sort every hour into four groups: customer understanding, decisions and strategy, team leadership, and coordination or reporting. Then ask three questions. Which group is largest? Which recurring tasks in the coordination group could an AI assistant draft for you? And what would you do with five extra hours a week if you had them? Write the answer down, and protect those hours on next week’s calendar before anything else fills them.

How AI changes this

AI changes the product leader’s job in three ways, and it is worth being precise about each.

It removes toil. Synthesizing interviews, summarizing support tickets, drafting requirements, writing release notes, pulling data, monitoring competitors, preparing meeting briefs: all of these can now be done in minutes by a well-instructed assistant. A product manager who still does them entirely by hand is choosing to be slower than their peers.

It raises the bar on judgment. Because the first draft is now cheap, the value moves to knowing whether the draft is right. Maya’s research agent produced a plausible, well-written, wrong conclusion. The skill is not producing the summary; it is reading three tickets in full when the summary does not smell right. Product leaders need to become excellent editors of machine output: checking sources, spotting confident errors, and asking what the summary left out.

It changes what the team can attempt. A small team with good AI tooling can prototype, test and learn at a pace that used to require a much larger organization. That makes discovery cheaper and lowers the cost of being wrong early, which is good. It also makes it easier to drown in output, which is not. The constraint shifts from capacity to clarity: the team that knows exactly what problem it is solving will outrun the team with more tools.

What does not change: accountability, relationships and taste. An agent cannot be accountable for a product decision, cannot earn the trust of a skeptical chief medical officer, and cannot feel the difference between a product that is merely correct and one that people love. Those stay with you.

A practical rule I use with teams: delegate the first draft, never the final call. Let agents gather, sort, summarize and propose. Keep humans on decisions that affect customers, money, safety or people, and make sure a human has actually read the evidence behind each one.

Why SaaS, and why healthcare examples

Most of the principles in this book apply to any product. I focus on software sold as a service because the subscription model makes the product leader’s job uniquely continuous. There is no launch-and-move-on. Every month, customers decide again whether the product is worth paying for, and every release can raise or lower that answer.

The examples lean on healthcare because that is where I have spent most of my career, and because healthcare is a demanding teacher. It has every hard problem in one place: many stakeholders with different goals, a buyer who is rarely the user, heavy regulation, entrenched legacy systems, and real consequences when software fails. The lessons travel. If your product serves banks, schools, factories or retailers, swap in your own regulations and stakeholders and the frameworks hold.

chapters.title: Finding Problems Worth Solving
chapters.epigraph:
“People don’t want to buy a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole!”

— Theodore Levitt, quoting Leo McGinneva
chapters.html:
The scheduling problem that wasn’t

Brindlepath was founded to fix scheduling. Its founders had watched patients leave the hospital with a stack of follow-up appointments they could not keep: the cardiology visit set for a Tuesday when the patient’s daughter, the only driver in the family, worked; the physical therapy slot across town with no bus route. Readmissions followed. The founders built a clever tool that let care managers book follow-ups around a patient’s real-life constraints.

Hospitals liked the demo. Very few bought it.

When Maya joined, she spent her first three weeks shadowing care managers at two customer sites and one hospital that had said no. What she found was that scheduling was a symptom. The deeper problem was that after discharge, nobody clearly owned the patient. The inpatient care manager’s job ended at the door. The primary care office did not know the patient had been admitted. The specialist had a referral but no context. A well-scheduled appointment did not help if nobody noticed the patient had missed it.

The care managers did not describe it that way. They described a dozen small frustrations: phone tag, faxes that went nowhere, discharge summaries that arrived after the follow-up visit, patients who “fell off the radar.” Maya’s job was to see the shape underneath the complaints. Once she did, Brindlepath’s product strategy changed from better scheduling to clear ownership of every patient through every handoff, and its sales conversations changed from feature demos to a problem every chief nursing officer recognized.

This chapter is about finding that shape, before you spend a year building the wrong thing.

Why products fail

Products rarely fail because the team could not build them. They fail because the team built something the market did not value enough, at a price or cost that did not work, at a time when nobody was ready.

CB Insights, which has studied startup failures for over a decade, analyzed 431 venture-backed companies that shut down from 2023 onward. Running out of capital was nearly universal, cited in 70 percent of cases, but CB Insights is careful to note that it is usually the final cause of death, not the root one.1 Underneath it sat the familiar culprits: poor product-market fit, bad timing, and unit economics that never worked.

The lesson for product leaders inside established companies is the same. A new product line or major feature that fails rarely fails on engineering. It fails on the question this chapter is about: was this a problem worth solving, for people willing and able to pay for a solution?

Start with a problem statement

Every product effort should begin with a written problem statement. Not a solution statement dressed up as a problem (“Users need a dashboard”) and not a vision (“Transform care coordination”). A problem statement names who is affected, what they are trying to do, what gets in the way, and what it costs them.

A useful template:

[Who] need to [goal or job], but [obstacle], which leads to [consequence, ideally measurable]. Today they [current workaround], which falls short because [gap].

Here is Brindlepath’s original problem statement, and the one Maya wrote after her field work:

Before: “Care managers need a better way to schedule post-discharge appointments.”

After: “Outpatient care navigators at health systems need to know, within 24 hours, which recently discharged patients are now theirs and what those patients need. But ownership after discharge is unclear, and information arrives by fax, phone and portal days late. As a result, a meaningful share of high-risk patients miss their first follow-up visit, which drives avoidable readmissions that the hospital is penalized for. Today navigators work from spreadsheets and daily phone calls with inpatient staff, which do not scale past a few dozen patients and break whenever someone is out.”

The second version is longer, and much more useful. It tells the team who the user is (the outpatient navigator, not the inpatient care manager), what success looks like (knowing within 24 hours), what the business case is (readmission penalties), and what the real competitor is (a spreadsheet and the telephone). Every one of those facts will shape the product.

A good problem statement passes four tests:

  • It contains no solution. If it names a feature, rewrite it.
  • It names a specific person, not “users” or “the market.”
  • It describes a consequence someone cares about, in their terms: time, money, risk, outcomes.
  • It can be wrong. A problem statement is a hypothesis. If no evidence could disprove it, it is too vague to be useful.

Jobs, not features

The most durable way to understand a problem is to ask what job the customer is hiring a product to do. The jobs-to-be-done idea, popularized by Clayton Christensen, holds that people do not buy products for their features; they “hire” them to make progress in a particular circumstance.2 Levitt’s quarter-inch hole is the same idea, decades earlier.

Jobs have three layers:

  • Functional: the practical task. Know which discharged patients are mine today.
  • Emotional: how the person wants to feel. Confident that nobody is falling through the cracks on my watch.
  • Social: how they want to be seen. The navigator the physicians trust to have it handled.

Products that serve only the functional job are easy to copy and easy to replace. Products that serve all three become part of how someone sees their own work. Brindlepath’s navigators did not just want a list; they wanted to go home at night without the low-grade dread that a patient was in trouble and nobody knew.

When you interview customers, listen for the job behind the request. When someone asks for a feature, ask what they would do with it, and then what that would let them do, until you reach something they genuinely care about. That is usually the job.

Who has the problem, who pays, who decides

In consumer software, the person with the problem, the person who chooses the product and the person who pays are often the same. In business software they almost never are, and in healthcare the gap is extreme.

For a single Brindlepath deal, the cast typically includes:

  • The users: outpatient navigators and care managers, who live in the product every day.
  • The clinical champion: often a director of care management or a chief nursing officer, who feels the readmission problem and sponsors the purchase.
  • The economic buyer: a chief financial officer or chief operating officer, who signs off on the money and wants a return.
  • The technical gatekeepers: IT and information security, who must approve integration with the electronic health record and the handling of patient data.
  • The influencers: physicians, quality leaders and compliance officers, who can slow or stop a deal without ever being in the room.
  • The beneficiary who never logs in: the patient.

Each of these people has a different version of the problem. The navigator cares about her day. The chief nursing officer cares about readmission rates and staff burnout. The CFO cares about penalties avoided and headcount not added. IT cares about integration effort and security risk. A product strategy that speaks only to the user will win enthusiastic pilots and lose the purchase.

Map your buying group explicitly. For each role, write down what they need to believe to say yes, what would make them say no, and what evidence would convince them. You will use this map again for positioning in Chapter 4, for pricing in Chapter 6 and for go-to-market in Chapter 13.

How big is the problem?

Not every real problem is worth solving. You need some way to compare problems before committing a team to one. I use three questions:

  1. How often does it happen? A problem that occurs every day for every user beats one that occurs once a quarter.
  2. How much does it hurt? Measure in the customer’s currency: hours lost, money spent, risk carried, outcomes harmed.
  3. What are they doing about it now? If people have built elaborate workarounds, or are already paying for something imperfect, the problem is real and the budget exists. If they shrug, it may be real but not urgent.

Plotting candidate problems by frequency and severity gives you a quick, honest picture of where to focus. Figure 2.3 shows the exercise Maya ran with her team after the field work. The positions are from that exercise, using the team’s own scoring; they are illustrative, not survey data.

The original scheduling product addressed a real but occasional pain. The ownership problem was frequent, severe and expensive. The map made the pivot obvious in a way no argument had.

Sizing the market

Once you have a problem worth solving, estimate how many people have it and what they would pay. Investors and executives will ask for three numbers:

  • Total addressable market (TAM): everyone who has the problem, if you won every one of them.
  • Serviceable addressable market (SAM): the part you can realistically reach with your product, channels and geography.
  • Serviceable obtainable market (SOM): the share you can plausibly win in the next few years.

Build these numbers from the bottom up, not from analyst reports. Top-down estimates (“the care-coordination market is $X billion; if we get 1 percent…”) are easy to produce and impossible to act on. A bottom-up estimate starts with countable units and a price.

For Brindlepath, the bottom-up version looked like this: there are a few hundred health systems in the United States with enough post-discharge volume and readmission exposure to care; each employs a number of outpatient navigators and care managers; Brindlepath prices per navigator seat with a platform fee. Multiplying the number of target systems by a realistic number of seats and a realistic price gives a market estimate the sales team can build a plan around and the finance team can check. The exact figures matter less than the method: every number in the chain is something you can verify by talking to customers.

Know the real competition

When teams list competitors, they usually list companies that sell similar software. That is the smallest part of the competition. The biggest competitor for most new products is the status quo: the spreadsheet, the phone call, the weekly meeting, the person who “just knows.”

For Brindlepath, the competitive set included:

  • Direct competitors: other care-coordination platforms.
  • The incumbent platform: the electronic health record vendor, which offered basic care-management modules that were “good enough” for some buyers and already paid for.
  • The status quo: spreadsheets, shared inboxes and daily huddle calls.
  • Doing nothing: accepting the readmission penalties as a cost of doing business.

Each requires a different answer. Against direct competitors, you win on fit and outcomes. Against the incumbent platform, you win on depth and speed. Against the status quo, you win by making the cost of the workaround visible and the switch painless. Against doing nothing, you win only if the problem is urgent enough that someone’s job depends on fixing it.

When you study competitors, study their customers more than their features. Read their reviews, talk to people who chose them and people who left them, and find out what job they were hired for and where they fall short.

Constraints are part of the problem

Every market has rules that shape what a solution can be. In healthcare, they include privacy law such as HIPAA in the United States, the need to integrate with electronic health records through standards like HL7 and FHIR, clinical safety expectations and, for some software, medical device regulation. Fintech has its licensing and anti-money-laundering rules; education has student-privacy laws; most enterprise software faces security reviews and procurement requirements.

Treat these constraints as part of the problem definition, not as obstacles discovered at the end. Ask early:

  • What data will the product touch, and what rules govern it?
  • What systems must it connect to, and how open are they?
  • Who has to approve it before a customer can buy or deploy it?
  • Could any part of it be regulated as more than ordinary software?

The answers change your cost, your timeline and sometimes your entire approach. A product that needs deep integration with five different electronic health records is a different business from one that works on a standalone basis. Better to know before you build. Chapter 11 covers trust and compliance in depth.

Brindlepath in practice: sizing the problem

When Maya presented the new problem statement to the board, the first question was the one every board asks: how big is this? She answered with a bottom-up estimate, built with Priya Nair, the CFO, and checked against conversations with a dozen health systems.

The chain of reasoning was simple. The team counted the health systems in Brindlepath’s target regions with enough post-discharge volume and readmission penalties to feel the problem, and found a few hundred. Field interviews suggested that a typical system in that group employed somewhere between twenty and sixty outpatient navigators and care managers who would use the product. At Brindlepath’s planned price of $1,800 per seat plus a platform fee, a typical customer would be worth roughly $70,000 to $150,000 a year. Multiplying the number of reachable systems by a conservative share and a typical contract value gave a serviceable market in the tens of millions of dollars of annual revenue, before any expansion into physician groups or health plans.

The number itself mattered less than the conversation it enabled. Because every link in the chain was something a board member could question and a salesperson could verify, the debate moved from “is this big enough?” to “which assumptions are weakest?” The weakest turned out to be the number of navigators per customer, which varied widely. So the team made it a discovery question for the next round of interviews, and refined the estimate a quarter later.

The same exercise exposed something uncomfortable about the old scheduling product. Fewer buyers felt that pain strongly, the budget for it was smaller, and the record vendor’s module already did “good enough” scheduling for many. The bottom-up math, as much as the field work, made the case for the new strategy.

Common mistakes

Falling in love with a solution. Teams often start with an idea and then look for a problem to justify it. The tell is a problem statement that quietly describes the product. Brindlepath’s original scheduling tool was a solution in search of the real problem.

Asking customers what they want. Customers are experts in their problems and unreliable designers of solutions. “Would you use this?” invites a polite yes. “Tell me about the last time this happened” invites the truth.

Talking only to the people who like you. Existing champions confirm what you believe. Prospects who said no, and customers who left, tell you what you are missing.

Ignoring the buyer. A product that delights users but cannot win over the economic buyer, IT and compliance will collect enthusiastic pilots and few contracts.

Sizing the market from the top down. “One percent of a ten-billion-dollar market” convinces nobody who has sold enterprise software. Build the estimate from countable customers and a realistic price.

Discovering constraints last. Regulation, integration and procurement requirements discovered after the product is built can double its cost or delay it by a year.

Try this

Write the problem statement for the most important thing your team is working on, using the template in this chapter. Then show it to three people: a customer, a colleague in sales or customer success, and an engineer. Ask each of them one question: “What is wrong with this?” Rewrite it after each conversation. If the statement changes substantially, you have learned something important before spending another week building. Finally, add the buying group: list each role, what they need to believe, and the evidence that would convince them.

How AI changes this

AI is genuinely useful in problem discovery, as long as you use it for breadth and keep humans on depth.

Use AI to scan wide. An assistant can read hundreds of support tickets, app-store reviews, sales-call transcripts, forum threads and competitor release notes, and cluster them into candidate problems. Work that once took weeks now takes an afternoon. Treat the clusters as leads, not conclusions.

Use AI to pressure-test your thinking. Ask a model to argue against your problem statement, list the stakeholders you have missed, or role-play a skeptical CFO. It will not always be right, but it is a fast, tireless sparring partner.

Use AI to draft the market model. Give it your bottom-up assumptions and ask it to build the spreadsheet and the sensitivity analysis. Then check every assumption yourself.

Do not use AI as a substitute for the field. A model trained on the internet knows what has been written about a problem, which is the average, often outdated view. The insight that changed Brindlepath’s strategy came from standing behind a navigator at 4:30 p.m. and watching her call three offices to find out who owned a patient. No dataset contained that. The most valuable discovery still happens in person, and it is the part of the job that AI makes more important, not less, because everyone else now has the same desk research you do.

Watch for synthetic certainty. AI summaries of customer feedback tend to smooth over disagreement and produce tidy themes. Real problems are messy. When a cluster looks too neat, read the raw material.

— Steve Blank
chapters.html:
Twelve navigators and a spreadsheet

Maya had a problem worth solving. She did not yet have a product, and she knew better than to let the team start building one.

Instead, she and Lena Park, Brindlepath’s head of design, recruited twelve outpatient navigators from three health systems: two existing customers and the hospital that had said no. They did not show them a prototype. They asked each navigator to walk them through the last three patients who had “fallen off the radar,” what had happened, when they had found out, and what they had done.

The stories were remarkably consistent. The navigator usually found out late, from the patient, a family member or an emergency department visit. The information she needed existed somewhere: in the discharge summary, the inpatient care manager’s notes, the specialist’s referral. It just never arrived in one place, at the right time, with a name attached.

Then Dev Raman, the engineering lead, did something that made the engineers on his team uncomfortable. Rather than build anything, he set up a shared spreadsheet for one navigator team at a customer site, and for two weeks a Brindlepath analyst filled it in by hand every morning: newly discharged patients, who the inpatient contact was, what the discharge summary said, and a suggested owner. The navigators used it every day. By the second week, they were asking for it before 8 a.m. One navigator caught two patients who would otherwise have been missed.

Nobody at the customer knew there was no software behind it. Two weeks and one analyst’s time had answered the most expensive question Brindlepath faced: if we deliver this, will they use it? Now the team could build with confidence.

Discovery is continuous, not a phase

In older ways of working, discovery happened once, at the start of a project, and produced a requirements document. Then the team built for months and found out whether they had been right.

Modern product teams treat discovery as a continuous practice that runs alongside delivery. Every week, the team learns something about its customers and tests at least one assumption. Teresa Torres calls this continuous discovery and offers a simple benchmark: a product team should be talking with customers at least weekly.1

Continuous discovery matters for three reasons:

  • Markets move. What was true at the start of a project may not be true at the end.
  • Small bets beat big ones. Testing an assumption in a week is cheaper than building on it for a quarter.
  • Teams that hear from customers make better small decisions. Hundreds of tiny choices about wording, defaults and edge cases go better when the people making them have heard real users recently.

The rhythm does not need to be elaborate. A product trio of a product manager, a designer and an engineering lead, holding one or two customer conversations a week and reviewing what they learned, will outperform most formal research programs.

Interviewing well

Customer interviews are the most important discovery tool and the most commonly done badly. The most common mistake is asking people to predict their own future behavior or to evaluate your idea. People are polite and optimistic. They will tell you your idea is great and that they would definitely use it. Then they won’t.

Rob Fitzpatrick’s rule of thumb is to talk about their life, not your idea; ask about specifics in the past, not generics or opinions about the future; and talk less, listen more.2 In practice:

Ask about the last time, not “usually.” “Tell me about the last patient you lost track of after discharge” produces a real story with real details. “How do you usually handle discharges?” produces an idealized process that matches the policy manual.

Follow the workaround. When someone mentions a spreadsheet, a sticky note or a daily phone call, ask to see it. Workarounds are evidence of a problem worth solving and a blueprint for the solution.

Ask what it cost. Time, money, stress, consequences. If they cannot name a cost, the problem may not be urgent.

Ask what they have already tried. Someone who has never looked for a solution probably does not feel the pain strongly enough to buy one.

Avoid pitching. The moment you describe your product, the interview becomes a sales call and the data becomes polite.

Interview the people who said no. Lost deals and churned customers teach more than happy ones. Maya’s most useful interviews were at the hospital that had rejected Brindlepath.

After each interview, capture the evidence while it is fresh: quotes, stories, workarounds and surprises, separately from your interpretation. Your interpretation will change; the evidence should not.

Map your assumptions

Every product idea rests on a stack of assumptions. Most teams never write them down, which means they never test them. A simple exercise changes that.

List every assumption that must be true for the idea to succeed, grouped by type:

  • Desirability: Navigators will check a daily list of newly assigned patients.
  • Usability: They can confirm or reassign ownership in under a minute per patient.
  • Feasibility: We can get discharge data from the customer’s health record within a few hours of discharge.
  • Viability: Health systems will pay per navigator seat, at a price that supports our margins.
  • Trust and compliance: Customers’ security teams will approve the data flow without a six-month review.

Then rate each assumption on two scales: how important it is (if it is wrong, does the idea fail?) and how much evidence you already have. The assumptions that are important and unproven are the ones to test first. This sounds obvious, yet many teams spend their first months polishing the user interface, the part they are most confident about, while the riskiest assumption, often a feasibility or viability question, waits untested until late.

For Brindlepath, the riskiest assumption was not whether navigators wanted a list. The field work had largely answered that. It was whether discharge data could flow from five different health record configurations quickly and reliably. So the team’s first technical spike was an integration test with one customer’s health record, not a user interface.

The evidence ladder

Not all evidence is equal. An enthusiastic comment in an interview is evidence; a customer changing their behavior is stronger evidence; a customer paying money is stronger still. Figure 3.1 arranges common validation methods by the strength of evidence they produce and the cost of running them.

The principle: match the strength of evidence to the size of the decision. A small feature change may need nothing more than a few interviews and a prototype test. A new product line with a dedicated team deserves evidence from the top of the ladder: commitments, pilots with success criteria, or paid pre-orders.

The experiments in detail

Interviews and observation. The base of the ladder. Cheap, fast and essential for understanding the problem; weak as evidence that people will adopt a specific solution.

Surveys. Useful for sizing a problem you already understand, measuring how widespread a behavior is or prioritizing among known options. Poor for discovering problems, and poor at predicting behavior.

Prototype tests. Put a clickable prototype in front of users and give them a task. You learn whether they understand the design and can use it. You do not learn whether they will use it every day.

Smoke tests. Describe a product or feature as if it exists, on a landing page or in an in-app prompt, and measure how many people try to use it or sign up. Common in consumer products; in business software, a “request early access” button for existing customers works well.

Concierge tests. Deliver the outcome by hand, openly, to a small number of customers. You learn exactly what the service needs to do, and whether customers value it enough to keep using it.

Wizard of Oz tests. Deliver the outcome by hand behind something that looks like a product, as Brindlepath did with its spreadsheet. You learn whether customers will change their behavior when the experience feels real.

Letters of intent and pilots with success criteria. A customer formally commits time, data or money to a trial with agreed measures of success and a decision date.

Paid pilots and pre-orders. The strongest evidence short of a full sale: someone gives you money for something that is not finished.

Minimum viable product, done right

The term minimum viable product is one of the most misused in the industry. It does not mean “the first release, with fewer features.” It means the smallest thing you can build that delivers real value to real users and lets you learn whether your core assumption is true.

Two words carry the weight. Minimum means you cut everything that is not needed to test the core value. Viable means what remains must genuinely work for the user; a broken or embarrassing product teaches you nothing, because users reject it for the wrong reasons.

There is good evidence that most teams build far more than they need. In a 2019 analysis of usage across 615 of its software customers, the product-analytics company Pendo found that 80 percent of features in the average product were rarely or never used, and that about 12 percent of features generated 80 percent of daily usage.3 The data comes from one vendor’s customers and is several years old, but it matches what most product leaders see in their own analytics.

Every feature that does not earn its place costs money to build, test, document, support, secure and maintain, for as long as the product exists. The cheapest feature is the one you were disciplined enough not to build.

Brindlepath’s MVP

After the spreadsheet test, Maya’s team defined the minimum viable product in one sentence: Every morning, each outpatient navigator sees the patients discharged in the past 24 hours who are now theirs, with the discharge summary and the inpatient contact attached, and can accept or reassign each one.

What they deliberately left out of the first release:

  • Scheduling, the original product’s core feature. Navigators could keep using the existing tool.
  • Analytics dashboards for managers.
  • Patient-facing messaging.
  • Support for every health record vendor. They started with the two configurations used by their pilot customers.

What they insisted on including, even in the MVP:

  • Role-based access controls and full audit logging, because patient data was involved and the customer’s security team would not approve anything less.
  • A way to reassign a patient in one step, because the field work showed ownership disputes were common.
  • A measure of the outcome: the share of high-risk discharged patients with a confirmed owner within 24 hours.

The list of exclusions is as much a part of the MVP as the list of features. Write it down, share it, and defend it.

Pilots that end in a decision

In business-to-business software, and especially in healthcare, validation often takes the form of a pilot. Pilots are valuable. They are also where many promising products go to die, in what people in the industry sometimes call “pilot purgatory”: a trial that is never declared a success or a failure and simply fades.

A pilot that ends in a decision has five things agreed in writing before it starts:

  1. The problem and the measure. What outcome are we trying to change, and how will we measure it? For Brindlepath: the share of high-risk discharges with a confirmed owner within 24 hours, and missed first follow-ups.
  2. The baseline. What is the measure today? If nobody knows, measure it before the pilot begins.
  3. The success threshold. What result would justify a purchase? Agree on a number, not on “a good result.”
  4. The scope and duration. Which teams, how many users, how long. Long enough to see the outcome; short enough to keep momentum. For most workflow products, 60 to 90 days is enough.
  5. The decision and the decision-maker. Who decides, on what date, and what happens next if the threshold is met: a signed contract, a wider rollout, a budget line.

Get the economic buyer, not just the enthusiastic user, to agree to these terms. A pilot sponsored only by the people who love the product will produce a happy report and no purchase order. Chapter 13 returns to pilots as part of go-to-market.

Brindlepath in practice: the pilot agreement

The spreadsheet test answered the desirability question. The next step was a pilot that could turn into a contract. Maya, Lena and the sales lead wrote a one-page pilot agreement with the second health system, using the template in the Appendix.

The measure was the share of high-risk discharges with a confirmed owner within 24 hours, along with missed first follow-up visits. The baseline took two weeks to establish, because nobody at the health system had measured it before: about 45 percent of high-risk patients had a clear owner within a day. The success threshold was 75 percent, sustained for the last four weeks of a 90-day pilot. The scope was one hospital and its outpatient navigator team of fourteen people. The health system paid a modest pilot fee and committed a navigator manager’s time each week. The decision-maker was the chief nursing officer, with the CFO’s agreement, and the decision date was written into the agreement, along with the price and timeline for a rollout to the system’s other four hospitals if the threshold was met.

Three things went wrong during the pilot, which is normal. The discharge feed missed patients from one unit for a week. Two navigators were on leave in the second month. And a change to the hospital’s risk-scoring rules briefly flooded the queue with low-risk patients. Because the pilot had a clear measure and a weekly review, each problem was caught and fixed within days.

By day 90, the measure stood at 82 percent. The decision meeting took twenty minutes, because nothing had to be negotiated: the terms had been agreed at the start. The rollout to four more hospitals began the following month.

Common mistakes

Running discovery as a phase. Teams that do a burst of research at the start of a project and then stop are surprised by what they learn at launch. Discovery is a weekly habit.

Pitching instead of listening. The moment you describe your idea in an interview, the data becomes polite. Save demos for later, and keep early conversations about the customer’s world.

Testing the safe assumptions. It is tempting to test what you are already confident about, such as the interface, while the riskiest assumption, often feasibility or willingness to pay, waits. Test the assumption that would kill the idea first.

Building an MVP that is all minimum and no viable. A product so thin that it does not solve the problem teaches you nothing, because users reject it for the wrong reasons.

Treating the MVP as the finished product. The opposite error: launching the first slice and moving on. An MVP is the beginning of learning, not the end of the project.

Running pilots without a decision. A pilot with no agreed measure, threshold or decision-maker drifts into “pilot purgatory,” consuming time and goodwill on both sides.

Try this

List the five assumptions your current idea depends on most, one each for desirability, usability, feasibility, viability and trust. Score each from one to five for how important it is and how much evidence you have. Pick the assumption with the highest importance and the least evidence, and design the cheapest experiment that could disprove it within two weeks. Use the evidence ladder in Figure 3.1 to choose the method. Then schedule the experiment, and decide in advance what result would change your plan.

How AI changes this

Discovery is one of the areas where AI helps most, and also where it can do the most damage if used carelessly.

Synthesis is now fast. Interview transcripts, support tickets and sales-call recordings can be transcribed, tagged and clustered by an AI assistant within hours of collection. A product trio that used to spend a week synthesizing a research round can now spend that week running the next one.

Prototypes are now cheap. AI coding and design tools can turn a sketch into a working prototype in an afternoon. That moves prototype testing down the cost axis of the evidence ladder and makes it reasonable to test several directions instead of one.

Humans talk; agents synthesize. The order matters. Use people for the conversations and the sense-making, and AI for the transcription, tagging, first-pass clustering and drafting. Figure 3.3 shows the division of labor that works in the teams I advise.

Synthetic users are not users. Some tools now offer AI-generated “personas” that answer interview questions. They can help you rehearse an interview guide or anticipate obvious objections. They cannot tell you anything true about your actual customers’ behavior, because they have never had your customers’ problem. Never count a synthetic interview as evidence.

Beware the smooth summary. AI is good at producing coherent themes from messy data, which is exactly the risk. Real customer evidence is contradictory and specific. Keep the raw quotes attached to every theme, and read a sample of the source material yourself. The navigator who caught two patients in the spreadsheet test is worth more than any summary of her.

Keep the patient’s privacy in mind. In healthcare and other regulated settings, interview recordings and support tickets may contain personal or health information. Before you put them into any AI tool, confirm that the tool is approved for that data, and remove identifying details where you can. Chapter 11 covers this in depth.

“The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do.”

— Michael Porter
chapters.html:
Three visions in one room

Six weeks after Maya Smith joined Brindlepath, the company held its annual planning offsite. By lunch on the first day, it was clear the leadership team did not share a picture of the future.

The CEO wanted Brindlepath to become “the operating system for care coordination,” a platform that every team in a health system would use. The head of sales wanted a product that could win the forty open opportunities in the pipeline, most of which were asking for scheduling improvements and a patient app. The chief medical officer, who had joined from a large health system, wanted the company to focus narrowly on high-risk patients after discharge, where the clinical evidence was strongest and the readmission penalties gave buyers a reason to act.

All three were reasonable. All three were, in their own way, strategies. And because nobody had chosen among them, the product team had been trying to serve all three at once, which is to say, none of them well.

On the second morning, Maya put a single page on the screen. It did not contain a roadmap. It contained a diagnosis of the market, one choice about where Brindlepath would play, one claim about how it would win, and a short list of things the company would stop doing. The argument that followed was the most productive two hours of the offsite.

This chapter is about writing that page, and about the work that makes it true.

Vision, strategy, roadmap: getting the words straight

Few words in business are used as loosely as vision and strategy. Teams waste hours arguing past each other because one person’s strategy is another’s roadmap. A simple cascade helps.

  • Vision describes the future you are trying to create for customers, usually three to ten years out. It answers why are we here? It should change rarely.
  • Strategy is the set of choices about how you will get there: which customers and problems you will focus on, and how you will win against the alternatives. It answers where will we play and how will we win? It is reviewed every year or so, and changes when the market does.
  • Outcomes are the measurable results that tell you the strategy is working: adoption, retention, revenue, the customer’s own results. They answer how will we know? They are set quarterly or half-yearly.
  • Roadmap is the sequence of bets the team will make to move those outcomes. It answers what will we try, in what order? It changes as you learn.
  • Backlog is the detailed work to deliver the current bets. It changes every week.

The common failure is to skip the middle: a lofty vision on a slide, a detailed backlog in a ticketing tool, and nothing in between that explains why this backlog serves that vision. When the middle is missing, every stakeholder fills it with their own strategy, which is exactly what had happened at Brindlepath.

Writing a vision people can use

A useful product vision has four properties.

It describes the customer’s world, not your product. “Brindlepath is the leading care-coordination platform” is about you. “No patient leaves the hospital without someone who owns their next step” is about the world you want to create. The second is far more useful, because it lets people judge any idea against a simple question: does this help make that true?

It is ambitious but believable. A vision nobody believes is decoration. A vision that is already true is a status report.

It is short enough to remember. If people cannot repeat it after hearing it twice, it will not guide their decisions.

It is concrete enough to say no. “Improve healthcare” excludes nothing. “Every patient has an owner through every handoff” excludes a great deal, including, as Brindlepath discovered, building a better scheduling tool for its own sake.

A good test: show the vision to a new engineer and ask them to name two things it rules out. If they cannot, it is too vague.

Strategy is a set of choices

The best short definition of strategy I know comes from Richard Rumelt, who argues that good strategy has a simple core: a diagnosis of the challenge, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and a set of coherent actions that carry out the policy.1 Bad strategy, by contrast, is a list of goals, a pile of fluffy language, or a refusal to choose.

Applied to product, the three parts look like this:

Diagnosis. What is really going on in the market, and what is the hardest problem we face? Brindlepath’s diagnosis: health systems are penalized for readmissions but have no reliable way to make sure someone owns each patient after discharge. Many vendors sell care-management modules, but few solve the handoff between inpatient and outpatient teams, because it requires integration with records, clear rules about ownership, and workflows that fit outpatient navigators. Brindlepath’s original product had spread itself across scheduling, messaging and reporting, and was not decisively better at any of them.

Guiding policy. What approach will we take? Brindlepath’s: become the best product in the market for owning high-risk patients in the 30 days after discharge, and prove it with outcomes, starting with health systems that face meaningful readmission penalties.

Coherent actions. What will we do, and stop doing, that follows from the policy? Invest in record integration and ownership workflows; build outcome reporting that a chief nursing officer can take to the CFO; stop new investment in the standalone scheduling product; decline deals that need a patient app as a condition of purchase; train the sales team to sell a problem, not a feature list.

Notice that the actions include things the company will stop doing. Michael Porter’s line at the top of this chapter is the most-quoted sentence in strategy for a reason. A strategy that does not make anyone unhappy has probably not chosen anything.

Where to play, how to win

A complementary lens comes from A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin, who frame strategy as an integrated set of answers to a few questions, the most important being where to play and how to win.2

Where to play covers which customers, which problems, which channels and which geographies. How to win covers the advantage that will make those customers choose you: a better outcome, a lower cost, a superior experience, a unique capability or a trusted brand.

The two answers must fit each other. Brindlepath could not win on price against the electronic health record vendor’s bundled module, and it could not win on breadth against large platforms. It could win on depth and outcomes in one specific, painful workflow. That determined where it should play: health systems where that workflow was a priority, not every organization that might buy care-management software.

Positioning: how customers should understand you

Strategy is what you decide. Positioning is how you help the market understand that decision. Even an excellent product fails if customers file it in the wrong mental drawer.

April Dunford’s framework is the most practical I have used. She defines positioning through five components that need to fit together:3

  1. Competitive alternatives: what customers would do if your product did not exist. Often the status quo.
  2. Unique attributes: the capabilities you have that the alternatives lack.
  3. Value: the benefit those attributes enable for customers, in their terms.
  4. Best-fit customers: the characteristics of the customers who care most about that value.
  5. Market category: the context you choose to present yourself in, which tells customers what to compare you with.

The order matters. Most teams start with the category and work backward. Dunford recommends starting with the alternatives, because your uniqueness only exists in comparison to something.

Brindlepath’s old positioning put it in the category “care-management software,” where buyers compared it, feature by feature, with large platforms and the record vendor’s module, and usually found it smaller. The new positioning put it in a narrower category, “post-discharge care transitions,” where the alternatives were spreadsheets, phone calls and modules that were not built for the handoff. In that frame, Brindlepath was not the smaller option; it was the specialist.

Positioning is not a tagline. It is the shared understanding that sits behind every tagline, sales deck, website page and product decision. Write it down, test it with customers and prospects, and expect it to change when your market does.

Communicating the vision and strategy

A strategy that lives in the head of the product leader is not a strategy. It is a hunch. The work of making it shared is less glamorous than writing it and far more important.

Write it on one page. If the strategy does not fit on a page, it is not yet clear. The page should contain the vision, the diagnosis, the guiding policy, the three to five most important actions, the outcomes you will measure, and what you will stop doing.

Tell it as a story. People remember stories, not bullet points. “A navigator at one of our customers found two patients last week who would have been missed” carries more weight than “improve post-discharge ownership rates.”

Repeat it until you are sick of it. By the time the product leader is bored of the strategy, most of the company has heard it once. Say it in all-hands meetings, planning sessions, customer calls and onboarding.

Connect every roadmap item back to it. When someone asks why the team is building something, the answer should trace back to the page in one or two steps.

Invite challenge, then decide. A strategy that has survived argument is stronger than one that was handed down. But a strategy that is re-argued every week is not a strategy. Hold a real debate, make the decision, write it down, and revisit it on a schedule rather than on demand.

The “not doing” list

The most powerful page in Maya’s offsite presentation was the last one: what Brindlepath would stop doing. It listed the standalone scheduling roadmap, the patient app, custom reporting for individual customers and two integrations requested by a single prospect.

Each item had a sponsor in the room. Each cut hurt. But the list did something no amount of prioritization could: it freed about a third of the engineering capacity for the work that mattered, and it told the sales team, clearly, which deals to walk away from.

Write your own not-doing list. Share it as widely as the strategy itself. It is the clearest evidence that you have a strategy at all.

Brindlepath in practice: the one-page strategy

Here is the page Maya put on the screen at the offsite, lightly edited.

Vision. No patient leaves the hospital without someone who owns their next step.

Diagnosis. Health systems are penalized for readmissions but lack a reliable way to make sure someone owns each high-risk patient after discharge. Care-management modules exist, but few solve the handoff between inpatient and outpatient teams. We have spread ourselves across scheduling, messaging and reporting, and are not decisively better at any of them.

Where we play. Health systems with meaningful readmission penalties and dedicated outpatient navigator teams, starting in our current regions.

How we win. Depth in one workflow: discharge data within hours, clear ownership, one-step reassignment and outcome reporting, proven with customers’ own numbers.

Guiding policy. Become the best product for owning high-risk patients in the 30 days after discharge, and prove it with outcomes.

Actions. Build the ownership queue and the standard record connector. Build outcome reporting for finance teams. Retrain sales to sell the problem. Move existing customers off custom integrations.

Outcomes. High-risk patients with a confirmed owner within 24 hours; renewal rate; time to first value.

Not doing. New investment in standalone scheduling; a patient app as a condition of sale; custom reports for individual customers; integrations requested by a single prospect.

The page was revised twice in the following year, both times on schedule. The not-doing list grew by one item and lost one: the patient-messaging need returned, but through an acquisition rather than a build, as Chapter 7 describes.

Common mistakes

Mistaking goals for strategy. “Grow revenue 40 percent” is a goal. A strategy explains how, given the market’s realities, you will achieve it, and what you will not do along the way.

Writing a vision about yourself. Visions that describe the company (“the leading platform”) inspire nobody and guide no decisions. Describe the customer’s world.

Refusing to choose. A strategy that tries to serve every segment, match every competitor and say yes to every request is not a strategy. It is a list of hopes.

Positioning against the wrong alternative. Teams compare themselves to the competitor they admire, while customers compare them to the spreadsheet they already have. Start from what customers would really do without you.

Strategy by slide. A strategy presented once at an offsite and never repeated does not exist for most of the company. Repetition is not redundancy; it is how strategy becomes real.

Changing strategy every quarter. Constant change looks agile and produces teams that never finish anything. Review strategy on a schedule, and change it when evidence demands it.

Try this

Write your product’s strategy on a single page, using the template in the Appendix: vision, diagnosis, where you play, how you win, guiding policy, three to five actions, outcomes and a not-doing list. Then run two tests. First, give it to a new engineer and ask them to name two ideas it rules out. Second, ask a sales leader to describe, from the page alone, the customer you should walk away from. If either test fails, the strategy is not yet clear enough to guide decisions. Rewrite it until both pass.

How AI changes this

AI is reshaping product strategy in three ways that every product leader needs to think through.

Features commoditize faster. When a capability can be built in days with a foundation model, a feature on its own is rarely a lasting advantage. Competitors, including the large platforms, can match a clever summarization or drafting feature within a quarter. Durable advantage moves to the things that are hard to copy: deep integration into workflows, proprietary data and feedback loops, trusted relationships, distribution, and the accumulated understanding of a specific customer’s problem. When you write your “how to win,” be honest about which of these you actually have.

New competitive alternatives appear. For many products, a general-purpose AI assistant is now a competitive alternative. A navigator might paste a discharge summary into a chatbot instead of buying specialized software. Your positioning has to explain why your product is better than that, and in regulated settings the answer often includes trust: privacy, accuracy, auditability and integration that a general tool cannot offer.

AI is a great sparring partner for strategy. Ask a model to attack your diagnosis, list the strategies a competitor might pursue, or argue for the opposite choice. Ask it to rewrite your vision in plain language, or to find the actions in your plan that do not fit your guiding policy. It will not make the choice for you, but it will help you see where your thinking is thin.

A warning: AI also makes it easy to produce strategy documents that sound impressive and choose nothing. Fluent prose about “leveraging synergies across the care continuum” is now free. A real strategy still requires a person willing to say no.

  2. A.G. Lafley and Roger L. Martin, Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works (Harvard Business Review Press, 2013).↩︎

  3. April Dunford, Obviously Awesome: How to Nail Product Positioning So Customers Get It, Buy It, Love It (Ambient Press, 2019).↩︎
