chapters.title: Prioritization and Outcome Roadmaps
chapters.epigraph:
“If everything is important, then nothing is.”

— Patrick Lencioni
chapters.html:
Two hundred and twelve ideas

The week after the offsite, Maya asked for an export of everything that had ever been requested of the product. The list had 212 items. Some were bugs. Some were feature requests from a single customer, logged three years earlier by a salesperson who had since left. Some were genuinely important. Eleven were labelled “top priority.”

The list was not a backlog. It was an archaeological record of every conversation the company had ever had. And it had been driving the roadmap, because the loudest recent request usually won.

Maya did three things in her first month. She archived every item older than a year that nobody could connect to a current customer problem; 130 items disappeared, and in the following year, nobody asked for any of them back. She grouped what remained under the outcomes in the new strategy. And she replaced the old roadmap, a list of features with quarter-end dates, with one organized around problems and outcomes, with dates only where a commitment was genuinely required.

This chapter covers how to choose what to work on, and how to show those choices in a way that builds trust rather than false certainty.

Output versus outcome

The most important shift in modern product management is from output to outcome. Output is what the team ships: features, releases, documents. Outcome is the change in behavior or results that the output was meant to produce: more navigators confirming ownership within 24 hours, fewer missed follow-ups, higher renewal rates.

Output is easy to measure and easy to celebrate. Outcomes are what customers and the business actually care about. A team can ship everything on its roadmap and change nothing that matters. Josh Seiden put it simply: an outcome is a change in human behavior that drives business results.1

Working on outcomes changes how a team behaves:

  • It starts each piece of work with a measurable goal, not a feature description.
  • It treats the first release as a test, not a finish line.
  • It stops or changes direction when the measure does not move, instead of shipping version two of something that did not work.
  • It talks about results in reviews, not just about what was delivered.

Outcomes are harder to commit to, because you cannot guarantee that a customer will change their behavior. That discomfort is honest. A roadmap full of committed features is promising something the team does not control: that those features will matter.

The outcome roadmap

A roadmap’s job is to communicate direction and sequencing, and to support decisions. It is not a release plan, and it is not a contract.

The simplest and most useful format I know is Now, Next, Later, a format associated with Janna Bastow and the team at ProdPad.2 Instead of dates on a timeline, items sit in three horizons:

  • Now: what the team is working on, with high confidence and detail.
  • Next: what comes after, with medium confidence; problems understood, solutions still open.
  • Later: what the team expects to tackle, with low confidence and no detail; mostly problems, not solutions.

Three features make this format work.

Every item is a problem or an outcome, not a feature. “Navigators can confirm ownership of discharged patients within 24 hours” leaves room for the team to find the best solution. “Build a discharge dashboard” does not.

Confidence is visible. Moving from Now to Later, the detail thins out on purpose. Stakeholders can see what is committed and what is a direction.

Dates appear only where they are real. Some commitments need dates: a regulatory deadline, a contractual obligation, a conference launch. Put those dates on the roadmap explicitly. Everything else is ordered, not dated.

Different roadmaps for different audiences

One roadmap rarely serves everyone. The board wants strategy and outcomes. The sales team wants to know what they can promise and when. Engineering needs sequencing and dependencies. Customers want to know whether their problem is being addressed.

Keep one source of truth and present it differently for each audience. Never show customers anything you would be uncomfortable being held to, and never give sales a date that engineering has not agreed to. The fastest way to lose a team’s trust is to promise their work to a customer without asking them.

Prioritization frameworks, and when to use them

Frameworks do not make decisions. They make the reasoning behind a decision visible, so it can be challenged and improved. Choose the framework that fits the decision.

RICE scores each option on Reach, Impact, Confidence and Effort: (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort. It was popularized by Intercom and works well for comparing many independent features where reach is measurable.3 Its weakness: it rewards things that touch many users a little over things that matter deeply to a few, and in business software the “few” are often the economic buyers.

Weighted scoring rates each option against criteria you choose, such as strategic fit, customer value, revenue impact, risk reduction and effort, each with a weight. It is flexible and makes strategy explicit. Its weakness: whoever sets the weights sets the answer.

Kano analysis sorts features into basic expectations (customers are angry if they are missing, but not delighted if present), performance features (more is better) and delighters (unexpected value). It is excellent for deciding what must be in a release and what will differentiate it.

Cost of delay asks how much value is lost for each week a feature is not available. Divided by duration, it gives weighted shortest job first, a sequencing rule popular in large organizations.4 It is the right tool when timing matters: a regulatory deadline, a competitor launch, a renewal at risk.

The same backlog can come out in a very different order depending on the framework. Figure 5.2 shows five Brindlepath candidates ranked both ways, using illustrative scores.

The lesson is not that one framework is right. It is that the choice of framework is itself a strategic choice, and should be made openly. If two methods disagree sharply on an item, that item deserves a conversation, not a formula.

The opportunity solution tree

For discovery-heavy work, Teresa Torres’s opportunity solution tree is a useful complement to scoring.5 It starts with the desired outcome at the top, branches into the customer opportunities (needs, pain points, desires) that could drive it, and only then into candidate solutions and the experiments that test them. It prevents the most common prioritization error of all: comparing solutions before agreeing on the problem.

The loudest voice in the room

Every product leader faces the same pressures: the CEO’s idea, the biggest customer’s demand, the deal that will close “if we just add this one thing.” Prioritization frameworks help, but the real skill is handling these conversations well.

For the executive’s idea: treat it as a hypothesis, like any other. Ask what problem it solves and what evidence would show it is working, and put it through the same discovery as everything else. Executives usually respect a product leader who takes their idea seriously enough to test it.

For the biggest customer: separate the need from the request, as in Chapter 1. Then ask whether the need is shared by other customers in your target segment. If it is, it may belong on the roadmap. If it is unique, consider whether it is better solved by configuration, a services engagement or a partner, rather than core product.

For the deal that needs one more feature: ask how many deals the feature has really decided in the past year. Sales teams are sincere, but every lost deal has many reasons, and the missing feature is the easiest one to name. Track requests by deal and outcome, and the pattern usually becomes clear.

When you say no, say it with reasons and an alternative: “We’re not building that this half, because our focus is post-discharge ownership. Here’s what we can do instead, and here’s when we’ll revisit it.” A clear, reasoned no builds more trust than a vague maybe.

Making room for what keeps the lights on

A roadmap full of new features eventually collapses under its own weight. Technical debt, security work, performance, and maintenance of what already exists all need capacity, and they rarely win a head-to-head scoring contest against a shiny feature.

The fix is to allocate capacity explicitly before prioritizing within each bucket. Figure 5.3 shows the split Maya agreed with Dev Raman for Brindlepath’s next two quarters.

The exact split depends on the product’s stage and health. A young product may put most of its capacity into new outcomes; a mature product with aging infrastructure may need far more for reliability. What matters is that the split is a decision made in daylight, reviewed each quarter, rather than the result of a hundred small trade-offs nobody saw.

Brindlepath in practice: one hard no

Six months after the new roadmap, Brindlepath’s largest prospect, a health system that would have doubled the company’s revenue in its region, asked for a patient-facing mobile app as a condition of purchase. The request came with a deadline: the app had to be live within six months.

The sales team argued for it, reasonably: the deal was large, and a patient app was on the “Later” list anyway. Maya ran the request through the same process as everything else. She asked what problem the app would solve for the prospect, and learned that the real need was a way to confirm patients’ contact details and preferred call times after discharge. She checked the evidence: none of Brindlepath’s existing customers had asked for an app, and two had said patients rarely downloaded them. She estimated the cost: at least two-thirds of a team for six months, displacing the standard connector that every existing customer needed.

The answer was no to the app, and yes to the need. Brindlepath offered a short text-message confirmation flow, built on the recently acquired messaging tool, which could be live in eight weeks and served the same purpose. Maya joined the sales call herself to explain the reasoning: the prospect’s patients would get what they needed sooner, and the prospect would be buying a product whose roadmap was not hostage to any single customer, including them.

The prospect signed, three months later, without the app. Not every hard no ends that well. But a reasoned no with an alternative ends well far more often than sales teams fear, and a roadmap that bends to every large request does not stay a roadmap for long.

Common mistakes

Treating the roadmap as a promise. Dates on features become commitments customers hold you to, whether or not the features turn out to matter. Commit to outcomes and to the few dates that are genuinely required.

Letting the backlog become a museum. A backlog of hundreds of items is not a plan. Archive anything no current customer problem supports; the important items will come back.

Scoring precisely, deciding badly. Frameworks produce numbers with decimal places that hide guesses. Use scores to structure the conversation, not to end it.

Saying maybe instead of no. “We’ll look at it” sounds kind and creates false expectations. A clear no, with reasons and an alternative, builds more trust.

Starving the foundations. Without an explicit capacity allocation, reliability, security and debt lose every head-to-head contest with new features, until an outage or breach forces the issue.

One roadmap for every audience. The board, sales and engineering need different views. A single document trying to serve them all usually serves none of them well.

Try this

Export your current roadmap and backlog. For each item, write the problem it solves and the measure it should move. Any item where you cannot do both goes into a “needs a problem” list for review. Then rebuild the roadmap in the Now, Next, Later format, with only problem-framed items, and mark the commitments that genuinely need a date. Finally, agree a capacity split with your engineering lead for next quarter, and write it at the top of the roadmap where everyone can see it.

How AI changes this

AI can do the bookkeeping. An assistant can de-duplicate a sprawling backlog, link requests to the customers and deals that raised them, draft RICE or weighted scores from available data, and summarize the evidence behind each item. Maya’s 212-item cleanup would take an afternoon today rather than a month. Treat the scores as a first draft. The model does not know your strategy unless you tell it, and it does not know which customer is about to churn.

AI creates roadmap pressure. Since 2023, almost every product team has faced demands to “add AI.” Some of those demands are right; many are a solution looking for a problem. Run AI features through the same discipline as any other: what outcome will this change, for whom, and how will we know? An AI feature that does not move a measure is an expensive demo.

AI features need different confidence. A traditional feature either works or it does not. An AI feature works some of the time, at a quality that varies with the input. Put AI items on the roadmap with explicit quality targets and evaluation plans, not just a ship date. Chapter 17 covers how.

AI can help you say no. Ask an assistant to write the case against your top three priorities, or to find the items on your roadmap that do not connect to your stated strategy. It is easier to hear an uncomfortable argument from a machine than from a colleague, and easier still to act on it before the planning meeting.

  2. Janna Bastow developed the Now-Next-Later roadmap format and popularized it through ProdPad, the product-management software company she co-founded.↩︎

  3. Sean McBride, “RICE: Simple prioritization for product managers,” Intercom blog, 2016.↩︎

  4. Donald G. Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow: Second Generation Lean Product Development (Celeritas Publishing, 2009).↩︎

  5. Teresa Torres, Continuous Discovery Habits (Product Talk, 2021).↩︎

chapters.title: The Numbers: P&L, Unit Economics and Pricing
chapters.epigraph:
“Price is what you pay. Value is what you get.”

— Warren Buffett
chapters.html:
What does a seat cost us?

In Maya’s second month, Brindlepath’s chief financial officer, Priya Nair, asked her a question in the hallway that she could not answer: “What does it cost us to serve one navigator seat for a year?”

Maya knew the price: Brindlepath charged per navigator seat, plus a platform fee per health system. She knew roughly what engineering cost. She did not know how much of the hosting bill, the support team, the implementation engineers and the integration maintenance each customer consumed. Nobody did. When Priya and Maya worked it out together over the following two weeks, they found that Brindlepath’s three smallest customers cost more to serve than they paid, mostly because each had needed a custom integration that the company now maintained for free.

That discovery changed the roadmap more than any customer interview. It also changed the way the CEO, the board and the sales team listened to Maya. A product leader who can explain the economics of a decision is a different kind of colleague from one who can only explain its features.

This chapter is the financial literacy that every product leader needs. It is not accounting. It is the handful of numbers that tell you whether your product is a good business.

Reading a SaaS P&L

A profit and loss statement, or P&L, shows revenue and costs over a period. For a software company, the structure is usually the same.

Revenue. For subscription businesses, the most watched figure is annual recurring revenue (ARR): the yearly value of active subscriptions. One-time revenue, such as implementation fees, is reported separately, because it does not recur.

Cost of revenue, also called cost of goods sold (COGS). The costs of delivering the service: hosting and infrastructure, third-party software embedded in the product, customer support, implementation and integration work, and, for AI products, model and inference costs.

Gross profit and gross margin. Revenue minus cost of revenue. Gross margin, gross profit as a percentage of revenue, is the single most important number for judging whether a software product is a good business. Mature software companies typically target gross margins well above 70 percent; services-heavy or infrastructure-heavy products run lower.

Operating expenses. Sales and marketing, research and development (where most product and engineering salaries sit), and general and administrative costs.

Operating income. Gross profit minus operating expenses. Many growing software companies run at an operating loss by choice, investing in growth. That is a strategy, not a failure, as long as the unit economics underneath are sound.

Figure 6.1 shows Brindlepath’s P&L in simplified form. The product leader’s influence is everywhere in it. Features that reduce support tickets raise gross margin. Integrations that need custom work for each customer lower it. A product that sells itself reduces sales and marketing cost. A product that needs a six-month implementation increases cost of revenue and delays revenue recognition.

Unit economics: is each customer worth it?

The P&L tells you how the business did. Unit economics tell you whether each new customer makes the business better or worse. Five measures matter most.

Customer acquisition cost (CAC). Total sales and marketing spend in a period, divided by the number of new customers won. In enterprise healthcare, where sales cycles run nine to eighteen months and involve many stakeholders, CAC is high.

Annual gross profit per customer. Average annual revenue per customer multiplied by gross margin. This is what a customer contributes toward paying back acquisition cost and funding everything else.

CAC payback period. CAC divided by monthly gross profit per customer: how many months it takes to earn back the cost of winning the customer. Shorter is better; investors often look for well under two years.

Retention. Gross revenue retention is the share of last year’s recurring revenue you kept from existing customers, ignoring upsells. Net revenue retention (NRR) adds expansion: upsells, extra seats, new modules. NRR above 100 percent means existing customers grow faster than others leave, which is the engine of the best software businesses.

Customer lifetime value (LTV). Gross profit per customer per year multiplied by the expected years a customer stays. The ratio of LTV to CAC is a common shorthand for the health of a growth model; a ratio around three or higher is a frequently quoted rule of thumb.

A worked example

Here is Brindlepath’s typical mid-sized customer after Maya and Priya finished their analysis. The numbers are illustrative.

  • 30 navigator seats at $1,800 per seat per year, plus a $36,000 platform fee: $90,000 annual recurring revenue.
  • Cost to serve, including hosting, support, integration maintenance and model costs: $22,500 a year, so gross margin is 75 percent and gross profit is $67,500 a year, or $5,625 a month.
  • Acquisition cost, including a long sales cycle and a pilot: $120,000.
  • CAC payback is therefore $120,000 ÷ $5,625, or about 21 months.
  • With gross revenue retention of 90 percent, the average customer stays about ten years, giving a lifetime gross profit of roughly $675,000 and an LTV-to-CAC ratio of about 5.6.

Figure 6.2 shows why product decisions are financial decisions. A self-serve pilot that shortens the sales cycle makes the dip shallower. Fewer custom integrations raise gross margin and steepen the climb. A second module that customers buy in year two bends the curve upward. A clunky onboarding that causes churn in year three cuts it off before it pays back.

The three small customers Brindlepath discovered were losing money for one reason: their custom integrations had pushed cost to serve so high that gross margin was close to zero. Their curves never crossed the line. The fix was not to fire them; it was to move their integrations onto Brindlepath’s standard connector, which became the first item on the Now column of the roadmap.

Pricing: the most underused lever

Pricing is one of the most powerful levers a product leader has, and one of the least studied. In a widely cited analysis of 2,463 companies, Michael Marn and Robert Rosiello found that a 1 percent improvement in price, with volume unchanged, increased operating profit by 11.1 percent on average, far more than the same improvement in variable cost, volume or fixed cost.1 Later McKinsey analyses of larger samples put the effect somewhat lower, at around 8 to 9 percent, but the conclusion holds: small changes in price have outsized effects on profit.

Price to value, not to cost

There are three broad ways to set a price. Cost-plus pricing adds a margin to what the product costs to deliver. It is simple and almost always leaves money on the table, because customers do not care about your costs. Competitor-based pricing anchors to what alternatives charge. It is necessary context, but it makes you a follower. Value-based pricing starts with the value the customer receives and captures a fair share of it.

For Brindlepath, value was measurable. A mid-sized health system with meaningful readmission penalties, a few hundred high-risk discharges a month and a goal of preventing even a modest number of readmissions could point to savings and avoided penalties many times the price of the software. That calculation, built with the customer’s own numbers, became the heart of every proposal. In the United States, the Medicare Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program can reduce a hospital’s base Medicare payments by up to 3 percent for excess readmissions,2 which gave finance teams a concrete number to put in the model.

The pricing metric

The pricing metric is the unit you charge for: per user, per seat, per transaction, per patient, per facility, per outcome. A good metric has three properties: it grows as the customer gets more value, it is easy to understand and predict, and it is hard to game.

Brindlepath’s per-navigator seat price was easy to understand but had a flaw: as the product made navigators more efficient, customers needed fewer of them, so success shrank revenue. The company added a per-health-system platform fee scaled by annual discharges, which grew with the size of the problem the product solved. Finding the right metric is often worth more than finding the right price.

Packaging

Most software is sold in tiers, often three, sometimes called good, better, best. Packaging decides which features go in which tier. Two principles help.

  • Put the features that define your best-fit customer in the middle tier, and price it to be the obvious choice. The top tier exists partly to make the middle look reasonable.
  • Use features to fence tiers that larger customers genuinely need, such as advanced security, audit reporting, single sign-on and integrations, rather than artificially limiting the core experience.

Pricing deserves the same discovery as features: interviews about willingness to pay, tests of different packages with new prospects, and careful analysis of win and loss rates by price point.

Making the business case

When you propose a significant investment, a new product, a major feature or an integration, bring a business case. It does not need to be long. It needs five things:

  1. The problem and the customers who have it, from your discovery work.
  2. The revenue effect: new customers won, expansion, churn prevented, price increase supported. Show your assumptions.
  3. The cost to build: engineering, design and product time, plus any third-party costs.
  4. The cost to run: hosting, support, maintenance, model costs, partner fees. This is the part most business cases forget.
  5. The risks and how you will know: what has to be true, and the measure you will check after launch.

Show a range, not a single number. A case that says “between $400,000 and $1.2 million of new ARR in the first year, most likely around $700,000, if pilots convert at our historical rate” is more credible, and more useful, than one that says “$1 million.”

Brindlepath in practice: changing the pricing metric

As Chapter 6 described, Brindlepath’s per-seat price had a flaw: the more efficient the product made navigators, the fewer seats customers needed. At one customer, a successful rollout had let the health system cover more patients with the same team, and its finance department asked, reasonably, whether it could reduce seats at renewal.

Maya and Priya spent a quarter on the problem. They interviewed finance leaders at eight customers about how they budgeted for the product and what they thought they were paying for. The answers were consistent: customers thought of Brindlepath as paying for covering their high-risk patients, not for navigator logins.

The new model kept a smaller per-seat price, to cover the cost of each user, and moved most of the value into a platform fee scaled to the number of high-risk discharges the product covered each year. For a typical customer, the total price stayed about the same in the first year. As customers expanded coverage to more hospitals and more patients, revenue grew with the value delivered, regardless of how many navigators they employed.

The team tested the model with new prospects before offering it to existing customers, and gave existing customers the choice to switch at renewal. Most did, because it made their budget easier to explain: the cost tracked the problem they were solving. Net revenue retention rose over the following year, and the conversation about reducing seats disappeared.

The lesson is not that platform fees are better than seats. It is that the pricing metric should grow with the value customers receive, and that finding it took the same discovery work as any feature.

Common mistakes

Pricing on cost. Customers do not care what your product costs to build. Cost-plus pricing systematically leaves money on the table for products that create real value.

Ignoring the cost to serve. Features that require custom work, heavy support or expensive AI calls can make customers unprofitable while revenue looks healthy.

Discounting to close. Deep discounts win this quarter’s deal and set expectations for every renewal. Discount scope or terms before price, and attach discounts to commitments.

Choosing a pricing metric that punishes success. If customers pay less as your product makes them more efficient, your growth works against you.

Business cases that forget running costs. A case that counts only the cost to build will overstate the return of almost everything.

Single-number forecasts. One revenue number invites false precision. A range with explicit assumptions is more honest, and more useful for decisions.

Try this

Pick one typical customer and calculate, with help from finance if you need it, their annual revenue, their annual cost to serve (hosting, support, implementation, integration maintenance and AI costs), their gross margin, the cost of winning them and their payback period. Then repeat the exercise for your smallest customer and your most demanding one. Compare the three. Most product leaders who do this find at least one surprise, and at least one roadmap item that would change the numbers more than any new feature.

How AI changes this

AI changes your cost structure. Traditional software has very low marginal costs: serving one more user costs almost nothing. AI features add a real variable cost for every request, paid to a model provider or for your own infrastructure. A feature that summarizes every patient record every morning can quietly add meaningful cost per seat. Track AI costs per customer, per feature and per request from day one, and put them in your gross margin. Products that lean heavily on AI often run at lower gross margins than traditional software for exactly this reason, so plan for it rather than discovering it.

AI changes pricing. When software does work that a person used to do, pricing per seat can undercut the value you create, as Brindlepath found. Many AI products are experimenting with usage-based pricing (per request or per task), outcome-based pricing (per resolved case or prevented readmission) or hybrid models. Each shifts risk between you and the customer. Outcome-based pricing is compelling to buyers and hard to administer; agree in advance exactly how outcomes will be measured.

AI makes analysis cheap. An assistant can build a pricing model, a cohort analysis or a business-case spreadsheet in minutes, and run the sensitivity analysis you would never have had time for. Use it. Then check the formulas, because a confident spreadsheet with a broken formula is worse than none.

Chapter checklist

  1. Michael V. Marn and Robert L. Rosiello, “Managing Price, Gaining Profit,” Harvard Business Review, September–October 1992. The figures are based on the average economics of 2,463 companies in the Compustat database. Later McKinsey analyses of the Global 1200 and the S&P 1500 put the effect of a one-percentage-point price improvement at roughly 8 to 9 percent of operating profit.↩︎

  2. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program. The maximum payment reduction is 3 percent of a hospital’s base operating diagnosis-related group payments.↩︎

chapters.title: Managing a Product Portfolio
chapters.epigraph:
“Management has no choice but to anticipate the future, to attempt to mold it, and to balance short-range and long-range goals.”

— Peter Drucker
chapters.html:
From one product to four

A year after the offsite, Brindlepath bought a small company that made a patient-messaging tool. The logic was sound: Brindlepath’s customers kept asking for a way to reach patients after discharge, and building it from scratch would have taken a year. Overnight, Maya went from leading one product to leading four: the core care-transitions product, an outcomes-reporting module that had grown up inside it, the acquired messaging tool, and the old scheduling product, which still had paying customers despite no longer being part of the strategy.

Each product had its own customers, its own technology, its own team and its own champion on the leadership team. Each wanted more investment. In her first portfolio review, Maya realized that the hardest question was no longer what should this product do next? It was how much should we invest in each product, and what should we stop?

That question is the subject of this chapter. Even if you manage a single product today, the habits here apply to the features and modules inside it, and they will matter the day your company grows a second product.

Products have life cycles

Every product moves through stages, and each stage calls for a different kind of investment and a different measure of success.

  • Introduction. The product is finding product-market fit. Revenue is small; learning is the main output. Measure learning velocity and early signs of retention.
  • Growth. The product has found fit and is scaling. Invest heavily in reach, onboarding and the features that unlock larger customers. Measure growth rate, net revenue retention and acquisition efficiency.
  • Maturity. Growth slows; the product is a reliable revenue and margin engine. Invest in efficiency, reliability, pricing and adjacent expansion. Measure margin, retention and expansion.
  • Decline. The market or technology has moved on. Invest only to keep customers safe and satisfied while you plan the exit. Measure cost to serve and migration progress.

The most common portfolio mistake is to manage every product the same way: the same planning cycle, the same metrics, the same expectations. A product in introduction judged on revenue will be killed before it has a chance. A product in maturity judged on growth will be pushed into features nobody needs. A product in decline that keeps its full team will consume resources the growth products badly need.

Mapping the portfolio

A portfolio map makes the investment conversation concrete. There are many versions. The classic Boston Consulting Group growth-share matrix plots products by market growth and relative market share.1 For software portfolios, I find it more useful to plot each product by its revenue growth and its gross margin, with the size of each bubble showing its revenue.

Figure 7.1 shows Brindlepath’s portfolio. The core care-transitions product is large, growing and healthy: the engine. The outcomes module is small, growing fast and highly profitable, because it reuses the core product’s data: a candidate for more investment. The messaging tool, newly acquired, is growing but at a low margin, because it pays a third party for every text message sent: it needs its unit economics fixed before it scales. The scheduling product is shrinking and barely profitable: a product to retire carefully.

None of those conclusions is automatic. The map does not make the decision. It replaces four separate pitches, each delivered with passion by a product’s champion, with one shared picture that the leadership team can argue about productively.

Three horizons

Portfolio thinking is also about time. The three-horizons model, introduced by Mehrdad Baghai, Stephen Coley and David White, sorts work by how far it is from today’s core business.2

  • Horizon 1 extends and defends the core business: improvements to the products that pay the bills today.
  • Horizon 2 builds emerging businesses that are starting to generate revenue and could become the next core.
  • Horizon 3 creates options for the future: research, experiments and early bets that may not pay off for years, if ever.

Companies under pressure tend to pour everything into Horizon 1, because it has the clearest return and the loudest customers. That works until the core business matures, at which point there is nothing ready to replace it. A deliberate allocation across horizons protects the future from the present. A frequently cited guideline, associated with Google in the 2000s, puts roughly 70 percent of effort on the core, 20 percent on adjacent growth and 10 percent on transformational bets. The exact split matters less than making it explicit and reviewing it regularly.

For Brindlepath, Horizon 1 was the core care-transitions product and its record integrations. Horizon 2 was the outcomes module and the messaging tool. Horizon 3 was a small team exploring AI agents that could draft a post-discharge plan for each high-risk patient for a navigator to review, a bet that, if it worked, could change the economics of care coordination entirely.

Platform and products

As a portfolio grows, the same capabilities appear in several products: user management, security, integrations, data pipelines, notifications, reporting, AI services. Building each one separately in every product is expensive and produces inconsistent experiences.

The usual answer is a platform: shared services that several products build on. Brindlepath’s most valuable platform capability turned out to be its record integration layer. Once it worked for the core product, the outcomes module and the messaging tool could use the same patient data without their own integrations, which cut implementation time for customers buying more than one product.

Platform work has a particular trap: it is easy to build a platform that nobody asked for, designed for imagined future products. The healthiest approach treats the platform as a product with internal customers. Extract shared capabilities from real products when two or more need them, rather than building them speculatively in advance.

Cross-selling and bundling

A portfolio creates new commercial options: selling additional products to existing customers, and bundling products together. Both can lift net revenue retention significantly, because selling to a customer who already trusts you is far cheaper than winning a new one.

But a bundle is only as good as the integration between its parts. Customers notice quickly when “the suite” is really three products with three logins, three data models and three support teams. Before you bundle, make sure the products share identity, data and design at least well enough that using them together is easier than using them apart.

Retiring a product well

Sooner or later, every portfolio needs to retire something. Brindlepath’s scheduling product had forty paying customers, a dwindling team and no future in the strategy. Keeping it alive cost more each year in maintenance and security work; shutting it down carelessly would damage trust with customers who also bought the core product.

A responsible retirement has five steps.

  1. Decide and explain why. Write down the reasons, the timeline and the alternatives customers will have. Share it internally first, so that sales and support can answer questions consistently.
  2. Give real notice. For business software, twelve months is a reasonable minimum; in healthcare, where changing a workflow requires training and sometimes clinical review, longer may be needed.
  3. Offer a path. Migration to another of your products, a partner’s product or an export of data in a usable format. Help customers move, especially your best ones.
  4. Handle data carefully. Regulated data has retention and deletion requirements. In healthcare, records may need to be kept for years after the product is retired. Plan how data will be returned, retained or destroyed, and document it.
  5. Free the capacity deliberately. Decide in advance where the team and budget will go. Otherwise, the savings from retirement quietly disappear into everything else.

Brindlepath migrated most scheduling customers onto a partner’s scheduling tool connected to the core product, kept a small number on an extended support contract, and moved the scheduling team into the record integration platform, where their knowledge of the health systems’ systems was invaluable.

Running portfolio reviews

A portfolio needs a regular rhythm of decisions, separate from the planning of individual products. Many companies hold a portfolio review each quarter. A good review covers:

  • Each product’s stage and its measures of success for that stage, not one common scorecard.
  • The portfolio map, updated with the latest numbers.
  • The horizon allocation, planned versus actual.
  • Shared platform needs and conflicts between products.
  • Decisions: where to add investment, where to reduce it, what to stop, and what to explore.

The output is a short list of decisions with owners, not a set of status updates. If a portfolio review ends without any product getting more or less than it had before, ask whether anything was actually reviewed.

Brindlepath in practice: the first portfolio review

Maya’s first formal portfolio review, a quarter after the messaging acquisition, ran for two hours with the CEO, CFO, head of sales and the leaders of each product. She sent the portfolio map in Figure 7.1 two days ahead, with a short page for each product covering its stage, its stage-appropriate measures and a proposed decision.

The core care-transitions product was in growth. Its measures were net revenue retention, time to first value and the North Star. Proposed decision: keep investing, with the standard connector as the priority.

The outcomes module was in introduction moving into growth: small, fast-growing and very profitable. Proposed decision: add two engineers and make it part of the standard package for new customers.

The messaging tool was in growth but with poor unit economics, because the per-message fees it paid a third party were not passed on to customers. Proposed decision: renegotiate the provider contract, add usage-based pricing for high volumes, and hold investment until gross margin passed 65 percent.

The scheduling product was in decline. Proposed decision: announce retirement with twelve months’ notice, migrate customers to a partner, and move the team to the integration platform.

The discussion was lively, and not every proposal survived intact. The CEO pushed back on retiring scheduling so soon; the compromise was fifteen months’ notice. The head of sales wanted the outcomes module offered at a discount; the decision was to include it in the standard package instead. But the meeting ended with a written list of decisions and owners, and the next quarter’s review began by checking them. That habit, more than any framework, is what turned a collection of products into a portfolio.

Common mistakes

One scorecard for every product. Judging a new product on revenue, or a mature one on growth, pushes both in the wrong direction. Measure each product on what matters at its stage.

Funding by volume, not evidence. The product with the most passionate champion often gets the most investment. A shared portfolio map makes the conversation about evidence instead.

Starving the future. Spending everything on Horizon 1 feels responsible until the core matures and nothing is ready to replace it.

Building the platform first. Shared capabilities built speculatively, for products that do not exist yet, are rarely what those products need. Extract them from real use.

Bundling before integrating. A suite that is three logins and three data models disappoints the customers you most wanted to impress.

Never retiring anything. Products in decline quietly consume maintenance, security and support capacity for years. Retiring them well frees investment for growth.

Try this

Draw your own portfolio map. If you have one product, use its major modules or customer segments. Plot each by revenue growth and gross margin, size it by revenue, and label its life-cycle stage. Then write one sentence for each: invest more, hold, fix or retire. Bring the map to your next leadership meeting and ask whether everyone agrees with the sentences. Where they do not, you have found the conversation the portfolio review should have.

How AI changes this

AI becomes a platform capability. Many companies are building shared AI services, such as model access, retrieval over their own data, evaluation tools and safety controls, that every product can use. Treating AI as a platform avoids each team building its own and makes cost, quality and compliance manageable. It is also a natural Horizon 2 or 3 investment for most portfolios.

AI can blur product boundaries. An AI assistant that can act across several products, answering a question by drawing on scheduling, messaging and outcomes data together, can make a collection of products feel like one. That raises the value of integrated data and shared identity, and the cost of a portfolio that is really separate products under one logo.

AI can disrupt your own core. The most uncomfortable portfolio question of this era is whether an AI-native approach could replace your Horizon 1 product. Brindlepath’s Horizon 3 agent experiment could, if it worked, make some of its own core workflow unnecessary. Better to discover that yourself, in a small team you control, than to read about it in a competitor’s launch announcement.

AI makes portfolio analysis faster. Assistants can assemble the portfolio map, reconcile metrics across products, and summarize customer feedback product by product before each review. As always, the judgment about where to invest stays with the leadership team.

The team that shipped and the team that didn’t

When Maya Smith arrived at Brindlepath, the company had two product teams of about the same size and seniority. One shipped steadily, recovered quickly from mistakes, and had a reputation with customers for listening. The other shipped in bursts, argued constantly, and had lost two engineers in six months.

Maya’s first instinct was to look at skills. The struggling team had good people: a strong product manager, an experienced designer, talented engineers. What it lacked was harder to see. In meetings, the engineers rarely questioned the product manager’s requirements, then quietly built something different. The designer learned about features after they had been specified. Nobody admitted a mistake until it reached a customer. Decisions were relitigated in the hallway after they had been made in the room.

The healthy team was not more talented. It was safer, clearer and closer. Its product manager, designer and engineering lead met with customers together, argued openly about what to build, and wrote down what they decided. When something broke, the first question was “what happened?” not “who did this?”

Maya spent more of her first year on the struggling team’s dynamics than on any feature. It was the best investment she made.

The roles on a product team

A modern product team is small, cross-functional and long-lived. It owns a meaningful part of the product, a problem area or a customer journey, and has most of the skills it needs to discover, build and run solutions without waiting on other teams.

The core is the product trio: a product manager, a product designer and an engineering lead.1 Together they own discovery. They talk to customers together, decide together what to test, and share responsibility for the outcome. Around the trio sit the rest of the engineers and, depending on the product, specialists in data, quality, content, security or clinical practice.

Each role has a distinct center of gravity:

The product manager is accountable for value and viability: that the team works on the right problems, that solutions create value for customers and the business, and that the work fits the strategy. The product manager is not the boss of the team, and does not own design or engineering decisions.

The product designer is accountable for usability and the experience: that customers can understand and use what the team builds, and that it feels coherent with the rest of the product. Great designers are involved from the first customer conversation, not handed requirements to decorate.

The engineering lead is accountable for feasibility and quality: that solutions can be built, run, secured and maintained, and that the team’s technical choices serve the long term. The best engineering leads shape what gets built by proposing simpler or more powerful approaches the product manager had not imagined.

Specialists bring depth the trio lacks. In healthcare, a clinical advisor, often a nurse or physician, can tell you in five minutes what would take five weeks of research to learn. A compliance partner involved early turns regulation from a late-stage veto into a design input.

The lines between roles are not walls. The best teams overlap generously: engineers who talk to customers, designers who understand the data model, product managers who can read a pull request. What matters is that accountability is clear, even when contributions are shared.

What makes a team effective

Between 2012 and 2015, Google studied over 180 of its own teams to find out why some were more effective than others. The researchers expected to find that the best teams had the best individuals, the right mix of skills or personalities, or the most experienced leaders. Instead, they found that how a team worked together mattered far more than who was on it.2 They identified five dynamics:

  1. Psychological safety: team members feel safe to take risks and be vulnerable in front of each other.
  2. Dependability: team members get things done on time and to a high standard.
  3. Structure and clarity: team members have clear roles, plans and goals.
  4. Meaning: the work is personally important to team members.
  5. Impact: team members believe their work matters.

Psychological safety stood out as by far the most important, underpinning the other four. The idea comes from Amy Edmondson’s research on hospital teams, which found that the best-performing units reported more errors, not fewer, because people felt safe to speak up about them.3 For a product team, psychological safety shows up as engineers who challenge a requirement before building it, designers who say “I don’t think this works,” and product managers who admit their hypothesis was wrong.

How a product leader builds safety

Psychological safety is not niceness. It is the confidence that you will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns or mistakes. A product leader builds it through small, repeated behaviors:

  • Go first on mistakes. Talk openly about your own wrong calls and what you learned. The team takes its cue from you.
  • Ask, then listen. “What am I missing?” and “What would make this fail?” are the most valuable questions in product management.
  • Separate the decision from the person. Critique ideas, not people. When something goes wrong, ask what happened in the system, not who is to blame.
  • Thank dissent. When someone disagrees in a meeting, thank them, even when you still disagree.
  • Close the loop. When someone raises a concern, tell them what you did about it, even if the answer is “nothing, and here’s why.”

Brindlepath’s struggling team improved within two quarters once its trio began meeting customers together and running blameless reviews after incidents. The engineers who had quietly built something different started saying so in the room.

Structure and clarity

Safety without clarity produces pleasant teams that do not ship. The other dynamics, especially structure and clarity, need deliberate work too.

Give each team a mission, not a feature list. “Make sure every high-risk discharged patient has a confirmed owner within 24 hours” gives a team room to think. “Build the ownership queue” does not.

Organize teams around customer problems or journeys, not technology layers. A team that owns “the navigator’s morning” can move faster than three teams that own the front end, the back end and the database, and must coordinate every change.

Make decision rights explicit. Who decides what to build, how it looks, how it is built, and when it ships? Write it down. A simple model is that the product manager decides what and why, design decides how it works for people, engineering decides how it is built, and the trio decides when it is good enough together.

Keep teams stable. Teams that stay together long enough to build trust and deep domain knowledge outperform teams assembled for each project. Move work to teams, not people to work.

Hiring and growing product managers

Hiring is the most important decision a product leader makes. A great product manager can make a mediocre team good; a poor one can make a great team miserable.

When I hire product managers, I look for five things above experience or industry background:

  1. Curiosity about customers. Do they ask about the people who use the product before they ask about the product?
  2. Clear thinking and writing. Can they explain a complex trade-off in plain language, on paper?
  3. Judgment under uncertainty. Given incomplete information, can they make a reasonable call and say what would change their mind?
  4. Influence without authority. Have they moved people who did not report to them?
  5. Ownership. Do they talk about outcomes they were accountable for, including the ones that failed?

The best interview exercises mirror the real work: a short written analysis of a product problem, a role-play of a difficult stakeholder conversation, a review of a real customer interview. Brain teasers and generic “design a product for X” questions tell you little.

Growing the team

Product management has few formal training paths, so most growth happens on the job. A product leader’s job includes building a development system:

  • Clear expectations by level, so people know what “good” looks like as an associate, a product manager, a senior product manager and a leader.
  • Regular coaching, focused on real decisions: reviewing a strategy document, debriefing a customer interview, preparing for a difficult conversation.
  • Stretch opportunities with support: owning a new area, leading a launch, presenting to the board.
  • A learning habit: shared reading, internal talks, and time for people to learn the domain deeply. In healthcare, that might mean shadowing clinicians every quarter.

Remote and hybrid teams

Most product teams now work partly or fully remotely. Google’s study found that whether teammates sat together had little to do with effectiveness. What matters is that the dynamics are deliberately supported.

Remote teams need more written communication, more explicit decisions, and more intentional connection. Write decisions down where everyone can find them. Use meetings for discussion and decisions, not status updates. Overlap working hours enough for real-time collaboration. Make customer conversations visible to everyone by recording them, with permission, and sharing highlights. And invest in occasional in-person time, especially for planning and for new team members.

Brindlepath in practice: turning a team around

The struggling team from the opening of Chapter 8 did not change because of a reorganization or a new hire. It changed through a handful of practices, introduced over two quarters.

First, the trio started meeting customers together. Every week, the product manager, the designer and the engineering lead joined at least one customer conversation, and spent fifteen minutes afterward agreeing what they had heard. Within a month, the engineers stopped quietly building something different from the requirements, because they had heard the same customers say the same things.

Second, the team adopted blameless reviews. After a production incident in which a configuration change hid patients from the queue for a morning, the review asked what in the system had allowed it, not who had made the change. The answer, a missing check in the release process, was fixed in a week. The engineer who had made the change led the review, which did more for psychological safety than any speech could have.

Third, the team wrote down its decision rights. A one-page agreement set out who decided what, and how disagreements would be escalated. Hallway relitigation dropped sharply once there was a clear place to raise a disagreement.

Fourth, Maya changed how she ran reviews. She stopped presenting conclusions and started asking questions: what are we missing, what would make this fail, what did we get wrong last time? She went first in admitting her own mistakes.

Six months later, the team’s anonymous survey scores on the five dynamics had risen on every one, most on psychological safety. Its delivery measures had improved too. The two engineers who had been considering leaving stayed.

Common mistakes

Hiring for résumé, not for the work. Impressive company names say little about whether someone can write clearly, make decisions under uncertainty and influence people they do not manage. Test the real work.

Handing requirements over the wall. A product manager who writes specifications and hands them to design and engineering loses the ideas those disciplines would have contributed, and their commitment.

Mistaking harmony for safety. Teams that never disagree are rarely safe; they are usually silent. Psychological safety shows up as open disagreement about ideas.

Reorganizing too often. Every reorganization resets trust and domain knowledge. Change team structures deliberately and rarely.

Bringing specialists in at the end. Clinical, security and compliance experts consulted only before launch can only say no. Consulted at discovery, they shape a better product.

Leaving growth to chance. Product managers who never get feedback or coaching plateau early. Development needs a system, not good intentions.

Try this

At your next team retrospective, ask everyone to answer five questions anonymously on a scale of one to five, one for each dynamic in Figure 8.2: Do I feel safe taking risks on this team? Can I count on my teammates? Are our goals and roles clear? Does this work matter to me? Do I believe it makes a difference? Share the averages with the team, without names, and discuss the lowest-scoring dynamic. Agree on one change to try for a month, then ask the same five questions again.

How AI changes this

AI joins the team as a tool, and sometimes as a teammate. Product teams increasingly work alongside AI assistants and agents that draft, analyze, test and monitor. The roles in Figure 8.1 do not disappear, but each role’s work changes. Engineers review more code than they write. Designers explore more options faster. Product managers spend less time on synthesis and status, and more on judgment and alignment.

Smaller teams can do more. A trio with strong AI tooling can prototype, test and ship at a pace that once required a larger team. That is an opportunity to keep teams small and focused, rather than a reason to cut them to the bone. The constraint that remains is human: the number of customer relationships, decisions and reviews a team can handle well.

New skills matter. Every role now benefits from knowing how to instruct, evaluate and correct AI tools, and how to tell good output from plausible output. Make this an explicit part of your development system, not something people pick up by accident.

Safety matters even more. When AI writes a first draft, people need to feel safe saying “this is wrong,” including when the draft came from a senior colleague’s prompt. And they need to feel safe admitting when they used AI and it failed. Teams that hide their AI use learn nothing from it.

Agents need owners. If your team deploys AI agents that act in production, someone must own each one: its instructions, its permissions, its quality and its failures. Chapter 17 covers how to lead teams that include agents.

  2. Google re:Work, “Guide: Understand team effectiveness,” describing Project Aristotle, Google’s study of more than 180 teams.↩︎

  3. Amy C. Edmondson, “Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams,” Administrative Science Quarterly 44, no. 2 (1999); and The Fearless Organization (Wiley, 2018).↩︎

The forty-page specification

Brindlepath’s first attempt at the ownership queue began the old way. A product manager on the struggling team, eager to get it right, wrote a forty-page specification. It covered every screen, every field, every edge case she could imagine. It took six weeks to write and two more to review. By the time engineering started, the design had changed twice, the pilot customer had changed its discharge workflow, and two of the edge cases had turned out not to exist.

The second attempt began with a two-page brief: the problem, the outcome measure, what was known and unknown, what was out of scope, and the open questions. The trio sketched three approaches together on the first afternoon, tested the most promising with four navigators that week, and had a working slice in a pilot customer’s hands within a month. The brief grew as the team learned, and by launch it was a clear record of what had been built and why.

The difference was not that the second team skipped the thinking. It was that they did the thinking together, in small steps, with customers in the loop, instead of alone, up front, in a document.

Requirements are a conversation, not a contract

A requirements document exists to create shared understanding across the team: what problem we are solving, for whom, how we will know it worked, and what constraints we must respect. It is not a contract between product and engineering, and it is not a substitute for talking.

The best requirements documents I have seen share five traits:

  1. They start with the problem and the outcome, not the solution.
  2. They separate what is known from what is assumed, and say how the assumptions will be tested.
  3. They state what is out of scope, as explicitly as what is in scope.
  4. They are short at the start and grow with learning, rather than being complete before work begins.
  5. They are written for the whole team, in plain language, not for a review committee.

Figure 9.1 shows the structure Brindlepath now uses for every significant piece of work. The full template is in the Appendix. The brief is the start of the conversation. User stories, designs, technical designs and test plans follow from it, written by the people closest to each.

User stories and acceptance criteria

For day-to-day work, many teams express requirements as user stories: short descriptions of something a user needs, written from their point of view. The classic form is: As a [type of user], I want [some goal] so that [some reason].

“As an outpatient navigator, I want to see which newly discharged patients are assigned to me so that I can contact the highest-risk ones first.”

A story is a placeholder for a conversation, not a complete specification. It becomes buildable through acceptance criteria: the specific conditions that must be true for the story to be done. Good acceptance criteria are concrete and testable:

  • Patients discharged in the past 24 hours appear in the queue within two hours of discharge.
  • Each patient shows risk level, discharging unit and inpatient contact.
  • The queue is sorted by risk level, then by discharge time.
  • Only patients assigned to the signed-in navigator, or to their team, are visible.
  • Every view of a patient record is logged for audit.

That last criterion is easy to forget and impossible to add cheaply later. In regulated products, privacy and audit requirements belong in acceptance criteria from the first story, not in a separate compliance phase.

Working with design

Design is not decoration applied at the end. It is the discipline of making the product understandable, usable and coherent, and it starts at the first customer conversation.

Involve design in discovery. Designers who hear customers firsthand make better decisions than designers who receive a summary. Brindlepath’s head of design, Lena Park, joined the navigator interviews in Chapter 3; her sketches from those sessions became the first prototype.

Explore before converging. Ask for several directions before choosing one. The first idea is rarely the best, and comparing options is the fastest way to find out what really matters to users.

Test with real users, early and cheaply. A paper sketch tested with three navigators teaches more than a polished mock-up reviewed by the leadership team.

Respect the design system. A shared library of components and patterns makes the product consistent, accessible and faster to build. Deviations should be deliberate, not accidental.

Design for the real environment. Brindlepath’s navigators worked on aging hospital computers, often with a headset on and a phone ringing. Small fonts, low-contrast text and multi-step workflows failed in that setting even when they tested well in a quiet conference room. Accessibility, which Chapter 11 covers, is part of this: design for the full range of people who will use the product.

Working with engineering

The relationship between product and engineering defines whether a team ships well. In healthy teams, product brings the why and the what, engineering brings the how, and both argue productively about the trade-offs.

Bring engineers in early. The best solutions often come from engineers who know what the technology can do cheaply that the product manager assumed was hard, or vice versa. Dev Raman’s suggestion to build the first version of the ownership queue on the hospital’s existing discharge feed, rather than a new integration, cut two months from the timeline.

Talk in outcomes and constraints, not tasks. “We need navigators to see new patients within two hours of discharge, and it must work with these two record systems” invites better solutions than “build a polling job that runs every five minutes.”

Make trade-offs visible. Every project trades scope, time, quality and cost. When something has to give, decide together what it will be, and write it down.

Protect quality. Pressure to ship always pushes against testing, security and reliability. A product leader who trades quality for speed without saying so is borrowing against the team’s future. Chapter 5’s capacity allocation exists so this trade-off is made deliberately.

Respect estimates as forecasts, not promises. Estimates are useful for sequencing and trade-offs. Treating them as commitments teaches teams to pad them.

From idea to release: the delivery flow

Most product teams today use some form of agile delivery: small increments of work, frequent releases, and regular reflection. The ceremonies vary, whether two-week sprints, continuous flow or something in between. The underlying flow is similar.

A few practices make the biggest difference.

Slice thin. Deliver the smallest piece of value that can be tested with real users, then grow it. The first slice of Brindlepath’s ownership queue showed only patient name, risk level and discharge time for one hospital unit. It was enough to learn whether navigators would use it every morning.

Release often. Small, frequent releases are less risky than large, infrequent ones, because each change is easier to understand, test and undo. Research by the DevOps Research and Assessment program, summarized in Accelerate, found that teams with high delivery performance deploy more often and have lower change failure rates: speed and stability go together rather than against each other.1

Separate deployment from release. Feature flags let teams deploy code without exposing it, then turn it on for one customer, one unit or a small percentage of users. In healthcare, where a change to a clinical workflow may require training or approval at the customer, this is invaluable.

Define “done” to include quality. A story is not done when the code is written. It is done when it is tested, secure, accessible, documented and measurable in production.

Measure delivery, but not just speed. The four delivery measures from Accelerate, deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service, balance speed with stability. Use them to improve the system, never to compare or rank individuals.

Launch readiness

A release is not a launch. A release puts code in production; a launch puts value in customers’ hands, with everything they need to use it. For significant changes, especially in regulated settings, a launch readiness review a week or two before launch saves a great deal of pain. It covers:

  • Product: acceptance criteria met, measures instrumented, known issues documented.
  • Quality and security: testing complete, security review done, privacy impact assessed.
  • Customers: release notes, training materials, and, for clinical workflows, any customer approvals required.
  • Support: support team trained, help articles ready, escalation paths clear.
  • Sales and marketing: positioning and messages agreed, as covered in Chapter 13.
  • Rollback: a clear plan to turn it off if something goes wrong.

The full checklist is in the Appendix.

After the release: learning

The work is not finished at launch. For every significant change, the team should know in advance which measure it expects to move, and look at it after launch. Did navigators confirm ownership faster? Did missed follow-ups fall? If not, why not?

Two practices help. A launch review a few weeks after release compares the result with the expectation and decides what to do next: iterate, expand, or stop. A blameless post-incident review after anything goes wrong asks what in the system allowed the failure, not who caused it. Both feed the team’s learning and, over time, its judgment.

Brindlepath in practice: thin slices

The ownership queue was delivered in five slices over three months, each one in a pilot customer’s hands within two weeks of the last.

Slice 1. For one hospital unit: patient name, risk level and discharge time, with a button to confirm ownership. No reassignment, no filtering, no reporting. The question it answered: will navigators open this every morning?

Slice 2. All units at the pilot hospital, with the discharge summary and inpatient contact attached. The question: does having the context in one place change how quickly navigators call?

Slice 3. Reassignment between navigators and teams. The question: how often does ownership change, and why?

Slice 4. Audit logging visible to the customer, role-based access by team, and the accessibility fixes found in testing. These were in the acceptance criteria from the start but were completed and verified here, before the second customer went live.

Slice 5. Outcome measures for the customer’s managers: owner within 24 hours, by team and by day.

Each slice was released behind a feature flag and turned on for the pilot customer when its navigators were ready. Two slices changed significantly because of what the previous one taught. After slice 2, the team learned that navigators wanted to see whether the patient had a follow-up appointment already booked, which moved up the roadmap. After slice 3, they learned that most reassignments happened on Monday mornings for weekend discharges, which led directly to the bulk reassignment feature.

The forty-page specification from the first attempt would have built none of those changes, and several things nobody needed.

Common mistakes

Writing the whole specification up front. A complete document before any learning guarantees that parts of it will be wrong, and that the team will feel bound to build them anyway.

Leaving non-functional requirements out. Privacy, audit, accessibility, performance and security are the requirements most often forgotten and most expensive to add later.

Treating estimates as promises. Teams that are punished for missed estimates learn to pad them, and the organization loses the information it needed.

Releasing big batches. Large, infrequent releases are harder to test, harder to understand when something breaks, and harder to roll back.

Calling it done when the code is written. Work is done when it is tested, secure, accessible, documented, measurable and in customers’ hands.

Never checking the result. A launch without a review of the measure it was meant to move teaches the team nothing about whether its judgment is improving.

Try this

Take the next significant piece of work your team will start and write a one-page brief using the template in Figure 9.1 and the Appendix, with the whole trio in the room, in under an hour. Pay special attention to two sections: “out of scope” and “must include.” Then write the acceptance criteria for the first story, and check that privacy, audit and accessibility appear in them. If writing the brief together surfaces a disagreement, you have saved weeks of rework by finding it now.

How AI changes this

AI drafts the paperwork. An assistant can turn a product brief into draft user stories and acceptance criteria, generate test cases from them, write release notes from merged changes, and keep the brief up to date as decisions are made. Review everything. AI-generated acceptance criteria often miss exactly the non-functional requirements, privacy, audit, accessibility and performance, that matter most in regulated products.

AI changes how code is written. AI coding assistants now write a large share of first-draft code in many teams. That makes prototyping and slicing faster, and puts more weight on code review, testing and architecture. A product leader should expect engineering to spend more time reviewing and less time typing, and should protect time for that review.

Prototypes get real. With AI design and coding tools, a working prototype connected to sample data can be built in a day. That blurs the line between discovery and delivery. Be explicit about which prototypes are throwaway experiments and which are the start of production code, because the quality bar is very different.

Requirements for AI features are different. An AI feature’s acceptance criteria are statistical: “summaries contain no fabricated facts in at least 99 percent of an evaluation set of 500 real discharge summaries, reviewed by a clinician.” They need evaluation sets, quality thresholds and monitoring in production. Chapter 17 covers this in depth.

Keep humans on the gates. AI can help at every stage of the delivery flow, but the quality gates, security review, clinical safety review and launch readiness, need accountable people.
