chapters.epigraph:
“Not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.”

— William Bruce Cameron
chapters.html:
Ninety-four charts

Brindlepath’s main analytics dashboard had ninety-four charts. Logins by day. Page views by screen. Average session length. Tickets by category. Each had been added by someone, for a reason, at some point. Nobody looked at most of them. When the CEO asked, at a board meeting, whether the new ownership queue was working, it took the data team three days to answer, because none of the ninety-four charts measured whether patients actually had an owner.

The problem was not a lack of data. It was a lack of agreement about which numbers mattered, and why. Maya replaced the dashboard with a single page: one measure that captured the value Brindlepath created for customers, four measures that drove it, and a handful of health checks. The page had eleven charts. People looked at it every day.

This chapter is about choosing the numbers that matter, collecting them well, and using them to make better decisions, without pretending that data can make decisions for you.

Data-informed, not data-driven

“Data-driven” is a popular phrase, and a slightly dangerous one. Data cannot tell you what you should want, which customers to serve, or whether a trade-off is worth making. It can tell you, with varying confidence, what is happening and sometimes why. The decisions are still yours.

A better phrase is data-informed: decisions are made by people, using evidence alongside judgment, strategy and customer understanding. Data-informed teams do three things well:

  1. They agree in advance what they will measure and why, so they are not tempted to find a metric that flatters the result afterward.
  2. They combine quantitative and qualitative evidence. Numbers say what is happening; conversations say why.
  3. They know the limits of their data: what it does not capture, how it could mislead, and how confident they can be.

Choosing what to measure

A North Star and its inputs

A useful approach, popularized by the analytics company Amplitude and by growth practitioners such as Sean Ellis, is to identify a single North Star metric: the measure that best captures the value your product delivers to customers, and that leads to long-term business results.1 A good North Star:

  • reflects value to the customer, not just activity;
  • leads revenue, rather than lagging it;
  • can be influenced by the product team’s work;
  • is understandable by everyone in the company.

For Brindlepath, the North Star was high-risk discharged patients with a confirmed owner within 24 hours, per month. It captured the core value, a patient someone was looking after, and it led directly to the outcomes customers bought the product for: fewer missed follow-ups and fewer avoidable readmissions.

A North Star on its own is too broad to act on. Below it sit a few input metrics: the measures teams can move directly, which together drive the North Star. Figure 10.1 shows Brindlepath’s metrics tree.

Each product team owned one or two inputs. The integration team owned discharges received within two hours. The navigator experience team owned patients reviewed by 10 a.m. and time to confirm or reassign. The adoption team owned active navigators per customer. Every team could see how its work connected to the North Star, and from there to the outcomes customers cared about and the revenue the business needed.

Other useful frameworks

Two other frameworks are worth knowing.

Pirate metrics (AARRR), introduced by Dave McClure, follow a customer through Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral and Revenue.2 They are useful for finding the weakest stage in a growth funnel, especially in products with self-service sign-up.

HEART, developed by researchers at Google, measures user experience through Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention and Task success, each paired with goals, signals and metrics.3 It is especially helpful for measuring the quality of a specific feature or redesign.

Whichever framework you use, the discipline is the same: start from the goal, decide what signal would show progress toward it, and only then choose the metric.

Beware vanity metrics

Vanity metrics go up and to the right and tell you nothing useful: total registered users, cumulative downloads, page views. They are easy to report and hard to act on. The test is simple: if this number changed, would we do anything differently? If not, it is decoration.

Brindlepath’s old dashboard tracked logins per day, which rose every month. It took a while to notice that much of the increase came from navigators logging in repeatedly because sessions timed out too quickly, which was a usability problem, not a success.

Retention: the number that tells the truth

For subscription products, retention is the most honest measure of value. Customers can be persuaded to buy once; they keep using and paying only if the product keeps helping them.

Cohort analysis shows retention clearly. A cohort is a group of users or customers who started in the same period. Tracking each cohort over time shows whether people keep using the product, and whether recent cohorts retain better than earlier ones, which is the clearest sign that product changes are working.

Look for two things in a retention chart. First, does the curve flatten? A curve that keeps falling toward zero means people are trying the product and leaving. A curve that flattens means a group has found lasting value. Second, are newer cohorts higher than older ones? If so, the product is improving.

In business software, measure retention at two levels: the user (are navigators still using it each week?) and the account (is the customer renewing and expanding?). Account retention lags user retention by months, so a drop in user engagement is your early warning.

Analyzing data well

Correlation is not causation

The most common analytical mistake is to treat a relationship as a cause. Customers who use the reporting module renew at higher rates. Does reporting cause renewal? Or do larger, more committed customers both use reporting and renew? Without more careful analysis, you cannot tell.

When the decision matters, find stronger evidence: an experiment, a comparison of similar groups, or a before-and-after analysis with a clear control.

Experiments

A/B tests, which randomly show different versions to different users and compare outcomes, are the strongest everyday tool for establishing cause. They work best when you have enough users, when outcomes can be measured quickly, and when showing different versions is acceptable.

In business software, and especially in healthcare, those conditions often do not hold. You may have a few hundred users per customer, outcomes that take months to appear, and clinical workflows where showing different versions to different nurses is inappropriate. Alternatives include staged rollouts across customers or units, with careful before-and-after comparison; pilot and comparison sites; and simple, well-designed observation of real use.

Whatever method you use, decide your measure and your success threshold before you look at the results.

Pair numbers with stories

Quantitative data tells you what is happening at scale. Qualitative evidence, from interviews, support tickets and session observations, tells you why. The best insights come from moving between the two. When the numbers show that navigators at one customer review far fewer patients than others, a single call with that customer usually explains why in ten minutes.

Building a measurement foundation

Good analysis depends on good data. A few foundations matter:

  • An event taxonomy: a consistent, documented set of events and properties that the product records, such as patient_assigned, owner_confirmed and patient_reassigned, with clear definitions.
  • Instrumentation as part of done: every significant feature ships with the events needed to measure its outcome, as Chapter 9 recommends.
  • One definition of each key metric, written down, so that “active navigator” means the same thing in every report.
  • Privacy by design: collect only what you need, avoid sending personal or health information to analytics tools that are not approved for it, and respect customers’ data agreements. In healthcare, analytics events should never contain patient identifiers unless the analytics system is covered by the right agreements and controls.
  • Self-service access for the product team to the data they need, with the data team supporting rather than gatekeeping.

Bringing financial and customer data together

The richest insights often come from joining product usage with financial and customer data. Which features do customers who expand use most? Which usage patterns predict churn six months before renewal? What does it cost to serve customers who use the product heavily versus lightly?

Brindlepath’s most useful analysis joined three sources: usage data, support tickets and contract data. It showed that customers whose navigators confirmed ownership for more than 80 percent of high-risk patients in the first 90 days almost always renewed, and those below 50 percent often did not. That single finding reshaped onboarding: the customer success team’s first goal became getting every new customer above 80 percent within 90 days.

Brindlepath in practice: finding the leading indicator

Brindlepath’s most valuable analysis started with a question from the CEO: could the company tell, months in advance, which customers were likely to renew? Renewal decisions came once a year, far too late to change anything. The team needed a leading indicator.

Maya asked the data team to assemble every customer’s history in one place: daily usage by navigator and site, the North Star and input metrics by month, support tickets, implementation milestones and contract outcomes. With only about forty customers at the time, the analysis was as much careful reading as statistics. The team plotted each customer’s ownership rate over its first year, colored by whether it had renewed.

The pattern was striking. Customers whose navigators confirmed ownership for more than 80 percent of high-risk patients within their first 90 days had, almost without exception, renewed. Customers that stayed below 50 percent through the first 90 days had mostly churned or renewed at a reduced scope. The middle group was mixed, and the difference usually came down to whether an executive sponsor had stayed engaged.

The team was careful not to overclaim. With forty customers, the finding was a strong signal, not proof, and it could reflect other differences between customers, such as how well-staffed their navigator teams were. So they treated it as a hypothesis and tested it: for the next ten new customers, customer success made reaching 80 percent within 90 days its first explicit goal, with weekly tracking and a playbook for customers who fell behind. Eight of the ten reached it, faster on average than any earlier cohort, and all eight renewed.

The 90-day ownership rate became the single most-watched number in customer success, appeared on the first page of every account review, and shaped the onboarding work described in Chapter 14. One well-chosen metric, built from joined data and tested before being trusted, did more than ninety-four charts ever had.

Common mistakes

Measuring what is easy instead of what matters. Page views and logins are easy to collect and rarely tell you whether customers got value.

Too many metrics. A dashboard with dozens of charts means nobody knows which ones matter. Fewer, better metrics get looked at.

Deciding the measure after seeing the results. Choosing the metric that makes a launch look good is a common, quiet way of fooling yourself.

Confusing correlation with cause. Customers who use a feature may succeed for reasons that have nothing to do with the feature.

Numbers without stories. Quantitative data shows what is happening; it rarely shows why. A single customer call often explains a puzzling chart.

Leaking sensitive data into analytics. Patient identifiers or other personal data in analytics events create privacy and compliance risk that far outweighs their analytical value.

Try this

Write down your product’s North Star metric and three or four input metrics that drive it, in the shape of Figure 10.1. For each input, name the team that owns it and the date it was last reviewed. Then open your main dashboard and remove, or move to a secondary page, every chart that does not connect to the tree. Finally, pick one input metric that moved unexpectedly last month and call two customers to ask what changed for them. Compare what they say with what the numbers suggested.

How AI changes this

Anyone can ask the data a question. AI tools that turn a plain-English question into a database query or a chart put analysis in the hands of everyone on the product team, not just analysts. That is powerful, and risky. The tool will happily answer a question built on the wrong definition of “active.” Shared, documented metric definitions, the foundation described above, become more important, not less, because AI tools should use them rather than invent their own.

AI finds patterns quickly. Models can scan usage data for unusual behavior, cluster users by how they use the product, and flag early signs of churn. Treat these findings as leads to investigate, not conclusions. Pattern-finding tools are especially prone to mistaking correlation for cause.

AI summaries need checking. An AI-generated summary of last month’s metrics may read beautifully and contain a wrong number. Any AI-produced analysis that will inform a real decision should show its sources and calculations, so a person can check them.

AI features need their own metrics. For AI features, measure quality, not just usage: how often the output is accepted, edited or rejected; how often it is wrong in ways that matter; and what it costs per use. Chapter 17 covers evaluation in detail.

chapters.epigraph:
“Security is a process, not a product.”

— Bruce Schneier
chapters.html:
The security questionnaire

Brindlepath’s largest deal of the year nearly died in a spreadsheet. The health system’s information security team sent a questionnaire with 312 questions: how data was encrypted, who could access it, how access was reviewed, how incidents were handled, where backups lived, which subcontractors touched patient data, and how the company knew its code was free of known vulnerabilities.

The sales team had expected the questionnaire to take a week. It took seven, because many of the answers did not exist yet. Engineering knew the data was encrypted, but nobody had documented how. Access reviews happened, but informally. The incident response plan was a page on the company wiki that had not been tested. Maya spent her evenings that month answering questions she wished the product had been designed to answer from the start.

The deal closed. Afterward, Maya made a change that outlasted any feature she shipped that year: security, privacy, compliance and accessibility became part of how every product decision was made, not a review at the end. Customers noticed. The next questionnaire took four days.

Trust is a product feature

The first edition of this book treated security and compliance mostly as regulatory obligations. This edition treats them as the fourth pillar of product leadership from Chapter 1: trust and responsibility. Customers buy software they trust. In healthcare, a breach, a privacy failure or a product that excludes people with disabilities is not just a technical failure; it is a failure of the product, and of the people who lead it.

The cost of getting it wrong is high and rising. IBM’s annual study of data breaches found that in 2025 the average breach cost $4.44 million across industries, and $7.42 million in healthcare, the most expensive industry for the fourteenth year running. Healthcare breaches also took longer to identify and contain: 279 days on average, against 241 across all industries.1

Those numbers measure only the direct costs. They do not capture the deals that never close because a prospect does not trust you, or the customers who quietly leave after an incident.

The landscape of obligations

Every industry has its own rules. The specifics change by country and over time, so treat this section as a map, not legal advice, and work with qualified counsel and compliance professionals.

In US healthcare, a product leader needs to understand at least these:

  • HIPAA and its Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules govern protected health information. Software vendors that handle it on behalf of providers or health plans are typically business associates and must sign a business associate agreement (BAA) with each customer, and with their own subcontractors that handle the data.
  • Interoperability and information-blocking rules from the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT shape how health data must be shared and accessed, and affect products that connect to electronic health records.
  • FDA oversight of software applies when software functions as a medical device. Some clinical decision support is excluded from device regulation when it meets specific criteria, including that clinicians can independently review the basis for its recommendations. Features that diagnose, treat or drive clinical decisions need careful regulatory analysis early.
  • State privacy laws increasingly add obligations for health and consumer data beyond HIPAA.
  • Accessibility requirements are tightening: in 2024, the Department of Health and Human Services finalized a rule requiring organizations that receive HHS funding to make their websites and mobile apps conform to the WCAG 2.1 Level AA standard, with compliance dates phased in from 2026.2

Beyond healthcare, most software sold to businesses must show its security practices through independent assessments such as SOC 2 reports, ISO 27001 certification or, in healthcare, HITRUST. Products sold in Europe must meet the GDPR, and AI features increasingly fall under new rules such as the EU AI Act, whose obligations are phasing in through 2027.

A product leader does not need to be a lawyer. They do need to know which rules apply, which product decisions trigger them, and when to bring in experts.

Security by design

Security by design means building security into every stage of the product’s life, rather than testing for it at the end. For a product leader, that means making sure the following happen as a matter of routine.

Threat modeling at design time. For every significant feature, ask: what data does it touch, who should be able to see or change it, and how could it be abused? Fifteen minutes with an engineer and a whiteboard catches problems that weeks of testing would miss.

Least privilege by default. Users, services and AI agents get only the access they need. Brindlepath’s navigators see only the patients assigned to their team; support staff can view a customer’s configuration but not patient records without an approved, logged request.

Strong identity. Single sign-on with customers’ own identity providers, multi-factor authentication, and prompt removal of access when people leave.

Encryption and audit. Data encrypted in transit and at rest, and every access to sensitive records logged in a way customers can review.

Secure development. Code review, dependency scanning, secrets management and regular penetration testing, built into the delivery flow from Chapter 9.

A tested incident plan. Know who does what when something goes wrong, how customers will be told, and how regulators will be notified. Then practice it.

Privacy by design

Privacy by design, a set of principles developed by Ann Cavoukian, starts from a simple premise: protect personal information by default, not as an afterthought.3 For a product team, it comes down to a few habits.

  • Collect the minimum. Every piece of personal data you collect is a liability as well as an asset. Ask whether you need it before you collect it.
  • Use data only for its stated purpose. Data collected to coordinate a patient’s care should not quietly become training data for an unrelated model.
  • Default to private. The most protective setting should be the default.
  • Be transparent. Tell customers, and where relevant patients, what you collect, why, and who you share it with, in plain language.
  • Plan for deletion. Know how long you keep data, and how you delete or return it at the end of a contract or a product’s life, as Chapter 7 discussed.

A privacy impact assessment for any feature that uses personal data in a new way makes these habits concrete. It need not be long: what data, for what purpose, with what risks, and what mitigations.

Accessibility is part of quality

Accessible products work for people with disabilities: people who are blind or have low vision, who are deaf or hard of hearing, who have motor or cognitive disabilities, or who rely on assistive technology. In healthcare, those users include patients, family caregivers and many clinicians.

Most software still falls short. WebAIM’s 2025 analysis of the home pages of the top one million websites found detectable accessibility failures on 94.8 percent of them, an average of 51 errors per page, most of them common and fixable problems such as low-contrast text and images without text alternatives.4

The international standard is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), published by the World Wide Web Consortium. Level AA of WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 is the common target. For product teams, accessibility is not a separate project. It is part of the definition of done:

  • Use a design system whose components are accessible by default.
  • Check color contrast, keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels and focus order for every new screen.
  • Test with assistive technology and, where possible, with users who rely on it.
  • Write in plain language. It helps everyone, including people reading under stress.

Accessibility also makes the product better for everyone. Brindlepath’s larger text and keyboard shortcuts, added for navigators with low vision, turned out to be popular with every navigator working a busy afternoon with a headset on.

Working with compliance as a partner

In many companies, compliance is the department that says no at the end of a project. That is usually because it was invited only at the end.

Invite compliance, security and, in healthcare, clinical safety partners into discovery. Share the product brief from Chapter 9 with them. Ask, early, which features will need their review and what they will need to see. Most compliance professionals would far rather shape a design than block a launch.

Build reusable answers. The 312-question security questionnaire taught Brindlepath to maintain a living trust package: security documentation, architecture diagrams, policies, audit reports and standard answers, kept current and shared with prospects early. Some companies publish a public trust center with much of this material. It shortens sales cycles and signals that you take trust seriously.

Brindlepath in practice: the trust package

After the seven-week security questionnaire, Maya asked a product manager to treat the company’s security and compliance documentation as a product, with customers (prospects’ security teams), a backlog and a release rhythm.

The first version of the trust package took six weeks to assemble. It included an architecture overview showing where patient data lived and how it moved; the company’s security policies; the results of its most recent penetration test and its independent security audit; a description of access controls, encryption, logging and backups; the incident response plan; a list of subprocessors that handled customer data, with their roles; the standard business associate agreement; an accessibility conformance report against WCAG 2.1 Level AA; and a library of answers to the hundred most common questionnaire questions, each with an owner and a review date.

Every new questionnaire became input to the backlog. Questions the package could not answer were added, and the gaps they exposed, such as an access review that had happened informally but was not documented, were fixed in the product or the process rather than papered over in an answer. When Brindlepath began using AI models, the package gained a section describing which models were used, for what, with what data, under what agreements, and with what evaluation and monitoring.

The results showed up in the sales cycle. The average time to complete a security review fell from about seven weeks to under two. Prospects’ security teams began telling Brindlepath’s sales team that the package was among the clearest they had seen, which, in a market where trust is everything, became a reason to buy. The work cost a fraction of one product manager’s time each quarter to maintain.

Common mistakes

Treating compliance as a final gate. Reviews at the end can only approve or block. Involving security, privacy and compliance early lets them shape a better design.

Collecting data just in case. Every field of personal data you store is a liability in a breach. Collect what you need, for a stated purpose.

Assuming the vendor handles it. Cloud providers and AI model providers secure their platforms, not your use of them. Responsibility for how your product handles data stays with you.

Leaving accessibility to a later release. Retrofitting accessibility costs far more than building it in, and excludes users in the meantime.

An incident plan nobody has practiced. The middle of a breach is the worst time to discover that nobody knows who calls the customer.

Overclaiming. Marketing claims about security, compliance or clinical outcomes that the product cannot support create legal and reputational risk.

Try this

Pick your product’s most sensitive workflow and walk through it with an engineer, a designer and, if you have one, a security or compliance partner. For each step, ask four questions: What personal data is involved? Who can see or change it, and should they? Is every access logged? Can someone using a screen reader or only a keyboard complete it? Write down every gap you find and add the fixes to your roadmap’s capacity for security and compliance. Then schedule a one-hour incident drill for the same workflow.

How AI changes this

AI features raise new trust questions, and product leaders own the answers.

Data flows multiply. Sending patient data to a third-party model provider is a new data flow with its own agreements, risks and obligations. In healthcare, the provider must typically sign a BAA, commit not to retain or train on the data, and meet your security standards. Map every AI data flow as carefully as any other.

New attack surfaces appear. AI systems can be manipulated through their inputs, for example by hidden instructions inside a document an agent reads, a technique known as prompt injection. Agents that can take actions need strict limits on what they can access and do, and human approval for anything consequential.

Outputs can be wrong, biased or unexplainable. A summary that invents a medication, a risk score that disadvantages a group of patients, or a recommendation nobody can explain are trust failures. Evaluate AI features for accuracy and fairness before launch and monitor them after, as Chapter 17 describes. Frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework offer a structured way to think about these risks.5

Transparency matters more. Tell users when content was generated by AI, show the sources behind it where possible, and make it easy for them to correct it. In clinical settings, make clear that AI output supports, and does not replace, professional judgment.

AI can also strengthen trust work. Assistants can draft answers to security questionnaires from your trust package, check new screens for common accessibility failures, review code for security issues, and summarize regulatory changes. As always, an accountable person signs off.

chapters.epigraph:
“Good design is as little design as possible.”

— Dieter Rams
chapters.html:
4:30 in the afternoon

The ownership queue tested beautifully. In usability sessions held in a quiet room at Brindlepath’s office, navigators found their patients in seconds, confirmed ownership in two clicks and rated the experience highly. Three weeks after launch at the first pilot site, usage had fallen by a third.

Lena Park went to find out why. She spent two days sitting beside navigators at the customer, from the start of their shift to the end. By mid-afternoon she understood. The navigators worked in an open-plan office with phones ringing constantly. They used aging computers with small screens, often with a headset on and a patient on the line. The queue’s confirm button was small and sat next to the reassign button; twice that afternoon, Lena watched a navigator reassign a patient by mistake and spend five minutes undoing it. Worse, the queue refreshed when new discharges arrived, so the list jumped under the navigator’s cursor in the middle of a call.

None of that showed up in the usability lab, because the lab was not the navigator’s world. The product worked. It did not work there.

The fixes were modest: a larger, separated confirm button, an undo for reassignment, and a queue that announced new arrivals instead of reshuffling. Usage recovered within two weeks and kept rising. The lesson cost Brindlepath a month. It is cheaper to learn it the way Lena eventually did: by going to where the work happens.

Empathy is a method, not a feeling

Empathy in product work is not about being kind or caring, though both help. It is a disciplined practice of understanding the people you build for well enough to anticipate what they need, often before they can say it. It has three parts:

  1. Context: where, when and under what conditions people use the product.
  2. Goals and emotions: what they are trying to achieve, what they fear, and what success feels like to them.
  3. Constraints: what limits them: time, training, technology, rules, other people.

In healthcare, the stakes of getting this wrong are high, and the people you design for are often exhausted. Clinicians already spend a large share of their day on screens. In a widely cited time-and-motion study of 57 physicians in four specialties, Christine Sinsky and colleagues found that only 27 percent of the office day went to direct clinical face time with patients, while 49 percent went to the electronic health record and desk work: nearly two hours of screen work for every hour with patients.1

Every product sold into that environment either adds to that burden or relieves it. Empathy is how you know which.

Methods for understanding people

Contextual inquiry. Watch people do their real work in their real environment, and ask them to explain as they go. This is the single most powerful empathy method, and the one most often skipped because it takes time and travel. Lena’s two days beside navigators found more than a month of lab testing.

Shadowing. Follow one person through a whole shift or day. You see the transitions, interruptions and workarounds that no interview reveals.

Journey mapping. Map the steps a person goes through to achieve a goal, including what they do, think and feel at each step, and where your product touches the journey. Journey maps make pain points visible to the whole team, including people who never meet customers.

Diary studies. Ask participants to record their experiences over days or weeks. Useful for understanding behavior that unfolds over time, such as a patient’s recovery after discharge.

Personas, used carefully. A persona is a short description of a type of user, based on research. Personas help teams remember who they are building for. They become harmful when they are invented, or when they replace contact with real people. A persona should be a summary of evidence, revisited when the evidence changes.

Designing for the real environment

Lena’s discovery generalizes into a few principles for products used under pressure.

Design for interruption. People will be pulled away mid-task. Save state automatically, make it obvious where they left off, and never lose work.

Prevent errors, and make them easy to undo. Separate destructive actions from common ones, confirm only when an action is truly hard to reverse, and offer undo everywhere else. Confirmation dialogs that appear constantly train people to click through them.

Keep the screen still. Do not move things under someone’s cursor. Announce changes; let the user choose when to see them.

Minimize clicks and typing for frequent tasks. A task done forty times a day deserves to be fast. Use keyboard shortcuts, sensible defaults and bulk actions.

Use plain language. Write for someone who is tired and distracted. Labels should say what happens, not what the system calls it.

Design for the hardware and the setting. Old screens, shared computers, gloves, glare, noise. Test on the actual devices in the actual place.

Design for everyone. The accessibility practices in Chapter 11 make products better for people with disabilities and for everyone working under strain.

The users who never log in

In healthcare, the person who benefits most from your product often never sees it. Brindlepath’s real beneficiary was the patient who went home from the hospital and needed someone to notice if things went wrong. That patient never logged in, but the product’s design affected them directly: how quickly a navigator called, whether the navigator had the right information, whether the follow-up visit happened.

Designing with empathy for the beneficiary means asking, at every decision, how it changes the experience of the person at the end of the chain. Brindlepath’s team began each design review with a short story of a real (anonymized) patient whose care depended on the workflow in question. It changed conversations. “This adds a step for navigators” became “this adds a step, and here is what it means for Mrs. Alvarez’s follow-up call.”

The same principle applies in other industries: the student behind the teacher’s dashboard, the customer behind the support agent’s screen, the citizen behind the government caseworker’s system.

Balancing empathy and innovation

Empathy keeps products grounded in real needs. Taken too literally, it can also keep them timid. Users describe their problems in terms of what they know, and their suggestions tend to be small improvements to today’s workflow. Breakthrough products often change the workflow itself.

The answer is not to ignore users, but to separate their problems, which you should trust deeply, from their proposed solutions, which you should treat as one input among many. Brindlepath’s navigators asked for a better spreadsheet. What they needed was for ownership to be assigned before they arrived in the morning, which no spreadsheet could do. The insight came from empathy; the solution came from the team’s knowledge of what technology could do.

A few practices help balance the two:

  • Test bold ideas with low-fidelity prototypes, so users react to the concept rather than the polish.
  • Introduce change gradually where workflows are safety-critical, with the option to use the old way during transition.
  • Measure whether the innovation actually relieves the burden, using time-on-task, error rates and the users’ own sense of workload.
  • Involve users as partners, not just test subjects. Brindlepath formed a small advisory group of navigators from three customers who saw designs early and helped shape them.

Continuous improvement for user-centricity

Empathy is not a phase. People’s work changes, products change, and the gap between them opens again. Keep it closed with a few lasting habits:

  • Regular field visits for every product trio, at least once a quarter.
  • A steady stream of feedback from support tickets, in-product feedback and customer success, reviewed by the product team weekly.
  • Usability measures for key tasks, tracked over time: completion rates, time on task, error rates.
  • Satisfaction measures used with care. Net Promoter Score and similar surveys can show trends, but a score without the stories behind it says little about what to fix.

Brindlepath in practice: the navigator advisory group

Lena’s discovery in the opening scene led to a lasting practice. Brindlepath formed a navigator advisory group: eight navigators and two navigator managers from four customers, who met with the product team for an hour every month and were paid a modest stipend, with their employers’ agreement, for their time.

The group saw designs early, usually as sketches or rough prototypes, before the team had invested much in any direction. They tested new workflows in their own environments for a week before wider release. And they brought problems the product team had not heard about: the navigator who covered a rural clinic with an unreliable connection, the manager who needed to rebalance workloads when someone called in sick, the new hire who could not tell which patients were most urgent on her first day.

Two rules kept the group useful. First, the product team presented problems and options, not finished solutions, and asked the group to argue about them. Second, the team closed the loop: every month began with a short review of what had changed because of the group’s input in previous months. Members said this was the reason they kept coming. Seeing their suggestions in the product made them advocates inside their own organizations, which customer success noticed in renewal conversations.

The group did not replace field visits or broader research. Ten people cannot represent every navigator. But it gave the product team a standing relationship with real users, and it caught several problems, including a confusing change to how risk levels were displayed, before they reached hundreds of navigators.

Accessibility in a real workflow

When Brindlepath ran its first full accessibility review of the ownership queue, it found problems no usability session had surfaced. The risk level was shown only by color, so a navigator with color blindness could not tell high from medium risk. The queue could not be used with a keyboard alone. A screen reader announced each patient row as “button, button, button.”

None of these was hard to fix. Risk levels gained text labels and icons. Every action gained a keyboard shortcut and a visible focus state. Rows were labelled with the patient’s name, risk level and discharge time. The fixes took one engineer two weeks, and the team added the checks to its definition of done so new screens would not repeat the mistakes. The keyboard shortcuts became one of the most popular features in the product, among navigators with and without disabilities.

Common mistakes

Testing only in the lab. Quiet rooms, fast computers and focused participants hide the interruptions, noise and fatigue of real work.

Inventing personas. Personas made up in a workshop reflect the team’s assumptions. Build them from research and revisit them when the evidence changes.

Designing only for the logged-in user. Patients, students, citizens and customers who never see the product are often the people it most affects.

Taking users’ solutions literally. Users are experts in their problems. Their proposed solutions are one input, often a modest improvement on today’s workaround.

Adding confirmation dialogs everywhere. Constant confirmations train people to click through them. Prevent errors by design and offer undo instead.

Equating empathy with satisfaction scores. A score shows a trend; it rarely tells you what to fix. Stories and observation do.

Try this

Arrange for every member of your product trio to spend half a day with a user in their real environment within the next month, watching rather than demonstrating. Each person should come back with three observations: one workaround, one moment of frustration and one moment where the product helped. Combine them into a simple journey map like Figure 12.2. Then pick the most painful moment on the map and make it the subject of your next round of discovery.

How AI changes this

AI can reduce burden, or add to it. The most promising AI features in healthcare, such as ambient documentation that drafts clinical notes from a conversation, aim directly at the screen time in Figure 12.1. But an AI feature that produces output clinicians must carefully check adds burden of a different kind. Design AI features around the reviewer’s time: make outputs easy to verify, highlight uncertainty, and make correction fast.

AI can scale empathy research. Assistants can transcribe and tag hours of field recordings, cluster support tickets by emotion and theme, and draft journey maps from research notes. That leaves more time for the field visits themselves, which no tool replaces.

Synthetic users are not users. As Chapter 3 warned, AI-generated personas can rehearse an interview guide, but they cannot tell you what it is like to be a navigator at 4:30 in the afternoon. Lena’s lesson does not change.

AI interfaces need empathy too. Conversational and agent-based features raise new design questions: how much the AI should do on its own, how to show what it did and why, how to let people stay in control, and how to avoid sounding more certain than it is. Chapter 17 covers these in depth.

chapters.title: Go-to-Market and Launch
chapters.epigraph:
“Marketing is not the art of finding clever ways to dispose of what you make. It is the art of creating genuine customer value.”

— Philip Kotler
chapters.html:
The launch nobody noticed

Brindlepath’s first big release after the new strategy was the outcome report: a view that showed a health system’s chief nursing officer and chief financial officer how many high-risk patients had been owned within 24 hours, how many follow-ups had been kept, and what that was likely worth in avoided readmissions. The product team was proud of it. It shipped on time, worked well, and was announced in a release note and a customer newsletter.

Three months later, four customers had opened it. The sales team had not mentioned it in a single deal. Customer success managers had not shown it in a single business review.

The report was not the problem. The launch was. Nobody outside the product team understood who the report was for, what it let them do, or how to use it in a conversation with a customer. Maya relaunched it properly: a one-page story for each audience, training for sales and customer success, a short demo built around a real (anonymized) customer’s numbers, and a target to show it in every quarterly review. Within a quarter, it was the most-requested part of every sales demo, and three customers used it to justify expanding to new hospitals.

The lesson is old, and every product team relearns it: building the product is half the job. Getting it into the hands and heads of the people it is for is the other half.

What go-to-market means

A go-to-market (GTM) strategy is the plan for how a product reaches its customers and wins their business: who you sell to, what you say, through which channels, at what price, and how you support them after the sale. It connects the strategy and positioning from Chapter 4, the pricing from Chapter 6 and the customer success work in Chapter 14.

A complete GTM plan answers six questions:

  1. Who exactly is the target? The best-fit customer profile and the buying group from Chapter 2.
  2. What is the message? The positioning, translated into language for each role in the buying group.
  3. How will they find and buy it? The motion and channels: direct sales, self-service, partners, marketplaces.
  4. What will it cost them, and how will they buy? Pricing, packaging, contract terms, procurement path.
  5. How will they succeed with it? Onboarding, implementation, training, support.
  6. How will we know it is working? Pipeline, win rates, sales cycle length, time to value, early adoption.

Choosing a motion

Software reaches customers in a few broad ways, and the choice shapes the product itself.

  • Sales-led. A sales team finds, qualifies and closes deals, often with long cycles and many stakeholders. Typical for large, complex, regulated purchases such as Brindlepath’s.
  • Product-led. Users discover, try and adopt the product themselves, often through a free tier or trial, and expand over time. Typical for tools that individuals or small teams can adopt without procurement.
  • Partner-led. Resellers, system integrators, platforms or marketplaces carry the product to customers. Common when a partner already owns the relationship or the channel, as Chapter 15 discusses.

Most companies end up with a blend. Brindlepath was firmly sales-led, but it learned from product-led companies: it made the pilot experience as self-explanatory as possible, so navigators adopted the product with little training, and their enthusiasm helped the sales team expand to other hospitals in the same health system.

Messaging for each audience

Positioning, from Chapter 4, is the shared understanding of what you are and why you matter. Messaging is how you express it to each audience, in their words, about their concerns.

For each role in the buying group, write three things: the problem they feel, the outcome they want, and the proof they need. For Brindlepath’s outcome report:

Audience Problem they feel Outcome they want Proof they need
Chief nursing officer Can’t show the board that care transitions are improving A clear, credible view of progress Their own data, trended over time
Chief financial officer Readmission penalties with no clear plan to reduce them A return on the investment Avoided readmissions, valued conservatively
Navigator manager Staff overloaded, no way to see where help is needed Balanced workload, fewer missed patients Patients per navigator, missed follow-ups by team

Test messages with real buyers before launch. Read them aloud in a customer’s voice. If a sentence sounds like a brochure, rewrite it until it sounds like something a customer would say to a colleague.

Building the launch plan

Not every release deserves the same launch. A useful practice is to tier launches by their importance to customers and the business, and match the effort to the tier.

A Tier 1 launch, a new product, a major capability or a change that shifts the company’s positioning, gets the full treatment: messaging for each audience, sales and customer success enablement, external announcement, customer events, and measures of success. A Tier 2 launch, a significant feature, gets targeted communication to affected customers and enablement for the teams that will discuss it. A Tier 3 launch, an improvement or fix, gets a release note and an update to help content.

Decide the tier when the work is planned, not the week before release, so marketing, sales and customer success have time to prepare.

Enabling sales and customer success

The sales and customer success teams are the product’s voice with customers. If they cannot explain a capability confidently, it effectively does not exist. Good enablement includes:

  • The story: a short narrative of the problem, the solution and the outcome, with a customer example.
  • The demo: a script built around a realistic scenario, not a tour of every button.
  • The objections: the hard questions customers will ask, with honest answers.
  • The boundaries: what the capability does not do, so nobody over-promises.
  • Practice: time for people to rehearse and ask questions, not just a slide deck in their inbox.

Pilots that become purchases

In business software, and particularly in healthcare, the path to a sale often runs through a pilot. Chapter 3 described pilots designed to end in a decision: agreed measures, a baseline, a success threshold, a fixed duration and a named decision-maker. From a go-to-market perspective, three more practices matter.

Price the pilot. Even a modest fee changes behavior. Customers who pay for a pilot assign people to it and take the decision seriously.

Design the pilot for expansion. Choose a scope that, if it succeeds, naturally leads to a larger rollout: one hospital in a system of five, one service line in a hospital.

Write the expansion terms in advance. Agree what happens if the success threshold is met: the price, scope and timeline of the full deployment. Then the decision at the end of the pilot is about results, not a fresh negotiation.

In the Brindlepath story, the share of pilots that became contracts rose from under half to about three in four once the company adopted these practices, and the time from pilot start to signed contract fell by several months. Your own results will depend on your market, but the direction is one I have seen repeatedly.

Launching in regulated markets

Launching in healthcare and other regulated markets adds steps a product leader must plan for:

  • Customer approvals. Health systems may require clinical, security, legal or IT review before a new capability can be turned on, sometimes for each hospital.
  • Training and change management. A change to a clinical workflow may need formal training and updated procedures at the customer. Feature flags, from Chapter 9, let you enable capabilities customer by customer when they are ready.
  • Claims and evidence. Be careful what you claim. Statements about clinical outcomes or cost savings should be supported by evidence and reviewed by legal and compliance. Use customers’ own results, with permission, rather than broad promises.
  • Contract and procurement timelines. Budget cycles, procurement committees and contract reviews can add months. Know your customers’ fiscal calendars and plan launches and pilots around them.

After the launch

A launch is a hypothesis about adoption. Check it.

Set measures before launch: how many customers will adopt the capability within 30, 60 and 90 days; how often it will appear in sales conversations; what share of eligible users will use it. Review them on schedule, and talk to customers who did not adopt to find out why. Sometimes the product needs work. Often, as with Brindlepath’s outcome report, the launch did.

Brindlepath in practice: relaunching the outcome report

The relaunch of the outcome report, described at the start of this chapter, followed the Tier 1 playbook.

The product marketing lead and Maya wrote a one-page story for each audience. For chief nursing officers: “Show your board that care transitions are improving, with your own data.” For CFOs: “See the value of avoided readmissions, calculated conservatively, with the assumptions shown.” For navigator managers: “See where your team needs help before patients are missed.”

The demo was rebuilt around a realistic scenario. A health system with five hospitals, one of them lagging, and a chief nursing officer preparing for a board meeting. The demo took eight minutes, and it ended with the question every buyer was actually asking: what is this worth to us?

The enablement session ran for two hours rather than the usual thirty minutes. Salespeople and customer success managers each demoed the report to a colleague playing a skeptical CFO, and the hardest questions were collected into an objections guide. The most common question, “How do you calculate avoided readmissions?”, got a careful, honest answer: a conservative method, the assumptions behind it, and a reminder that the customer’s own finance team should validate the figure.

Customer success set a goal to show the report in every quarterly review for the next two quarters, and tracked it. Three measures were reviewed at 30, 60 and 90 days: customers who opened the report, appearances in sales opportunities, and expansions where the report was cited.

At 90 days, the report had been opened by most customers, appeared in most active sales opportunities, and had been cited by three customers as part of the case for expanding to new hospitals. The product had not changed at all between the first launch and the relaunch. Only the launch had.

Pricing the pilot, in practice

Brindlepath’s early pilots were free, on the theory that removing cost would remove friction. It did. It also removed commitment. Customers assigned whoever was available, missed weekly reviews and let pilots drift.

The company began charging a modest fee for every pilot, credited against the first year’s contract if the customer went ahead. The effect on behavior was immediate. Customers assigned a named manager, protected navigators’ time for training, and came to decision meetings prepared. The fee was small enough that it rarely slowed a deal, and the few prospects who would not pay anything turned out to be the ones least likely to buy.

Common mistakes

Launching to the product team. A release note and a newsletter mention reach the people who already know about the feature. Customers and sellers need a story, a demo and a reason to care.

One message for everyone. The navigator, the chief nursing officer and the CFO care about different things. A single message usually speaks to none of them.

Enabling sales with slides. Sellers learn by practicing, not by reading. Give them a demo script, the hard questions and time to rehearse.

Free pilots with no exit. Unpriced pilots without expansion terms invite casual commitment and end in renegotiation rather than a decision.

Forgetting the customer’s calendar. Health systems and other large buyers have budget cycles, approval committees and training windows. Launches that ignore them stall.

Overpromising AI. Claims an AI feature cannot consistently meet damage trust far more than the feature builds it.

Try this

Pick your next significant release and write the messaging table from this chapter for it: each role in the buying group, the problem they feel, the outcome they want and the proof they need. Then give a salesperson ten minutes to demo the capability to you, cold, using only the materials you have prepared. Note every question they cannot answer and every claim they make that the product does not support. That list is your enablement plan.

How AI changes this

AI accelerates launch work. Assistants can draft messaging variants for each audience, release notes, help articles, sales talk tracks and training quizzes from the product brief. They can analyze win and loss notes and call transcripts to find which messages resonate. Review everything for accuracy, especially claims.

Launching AI features needs extra care. Customers, especially in healthcare, want to know how an AI feature works, what data it uses, how accurate it is, and what happens when it is wrong. Prepare clear answers, documentation of evaluation results, and guidance on appropriate use. Over-promising on an AI feature damages trust faster than almost anything else.

Buyers will ask about your AI posture. Even for non-AI features, many security and procurement reviews now include questions about how a vendor uses AI, where customer data goes, and whether it is used to train models. Add these answers to the trust package from Chapter 11.

AI changes how buyers research. Buyers increasingly ask AI assistants to compare vendors and summarize options before they talk to sales. Clear, specific, well-structured public information about what your product does and for whom helps you show up accurately in those answers.

chapters.title: Customer Success and Retention
chapters.epigraph:
“Your most unhappy customers are your greatest source of learning.”

— Bill Gates
chapters.html:
The renewal that almost wasn’t

Ninety days before Ambermoor Health’s renewal, Brindlepath’s customer success manager, Tomás Rivera, ran his usual review and found something alarming. Ambermoor was Brindlepath’s largest customer, and on paper everything was fine: no open escalations, a friendly relationship with the director of care management, and an invoice paid on time. But the usage data told a different story. At two of Ambermoor’s five hospitals, the share of high-risk patients with a confirmed owner within 24 hours had fallen from over 80 percent to under 40 percent in three months.

Tomás called the navigator managers at both hospitals. One had lost three experienced navigators to retirement, and the new hires had never been trained on the product. The other had changed how discharges were coded, so a third of high-risk patients no longer appeared in the queue at all.

Neither problem would have reached Brindlepath through a support ticket. Both would have shown up at renewal as a vague sense that “the product isn’t working for us anymore.” Instead, Brindlepath trained the new navigators, fixed the coding mapping with the hospital’s IT team, and walked into the renewal conversation with a chart showing both hospitals back above 80 percent. Ambermoor renewed, and added two more hospitals.

Customer success is the discipline of noticing those signals early, and acting before the customer has to ask.

Customer success is not support

Support responds when something is broken. Customer success works proactively to make sure customers achieve the outcomes they bought the product for, and keep achieving them. Support is reactive and measured by how quickly problems are resolved. Customer success is proactive and measured by retention, expansion and, above all, customer outcomes.

The distinction matters because subscription businesses live or die on retention. A customer who signs a contract has bought the right to decide again at renewal. Every month in between, the product either proves its value or erodes it.

Why retention compounds

Small differences in retention produce large differences over time. Figure 14.1 follows the same $10 million of annual recurring revenue over five years at three different rates of net revenue retention: the revenue you keep from existing customers, including expansion, as introduced in Chapter 6.

At 90 percent net retention, the base shrinks to about $5.9 million in five years, and the company must win more than $4 million of new business just to stand still. At 100 percent, it holds steady. At 120 percent, existing customers alone grow it to nearly $25 million. That is why the best software businesses invest heavily in the customers they already have: retention and expansion are usually cheaper than acquisition, and they compound.

The customer life cycle

Customer success follows customers through a life cycle, with different work at each stage.

Onboarding and implementation. The customer sets up the product, connects data and trains users. In healthcare, this often includes record integration, security review and clinical workflow changes. The goal is time to first value: how quickly the customer sees the outcome they bought. For Brindlepath, first value was the first week in which a hospital’s navigators confirmed ownership of more than 80 percent of high-risk patients.

Adoption. Users build the product into their daily work. Customer success tracks usage, finds teams or sites that are lagging, and helps them catch up.

Value realization. The customer achieves and can demonstrate the outcomes they bought: fewer missed follow-ups, fewer readmissions, saved time. Regular business reviews make this value visible to the executives who will decide on renewal.

Renewal. The customer decides to continue. Renewals should be a formality by the time they arrive, because the value has been shown throughout the year.

Expansion. The customer extends the product to more users, sites or modules. Expansion is the natural result of proven value, not a separate sales campaign.

Onboarding matters most

Of all these stages, onboarding has the largest effect on long-term retention. Customers who reach first value quickly tend to stay; customers who struggle through a long implementation often never fully recover their enthusiasm. Brindlepath’s analysis in Chapter 10 found that customers who reached 80 percent ownership within 90 days almost always renewed.

To shorten time to first value:

  • Define first value precisely, for each type of customer, and track it.
  • Remove setup work from the customer. Standard integrations, templates and sensible defaults beat custom configuration.
  • Start small. Get one team or site to value first, then expand.
  • Assign clear owners on both sides, with a shared plan and dates.
  • Celebrate first value with the customer’s executives, so they see it early.

Health scores: seeing trouble early

A customer health score combines several signals into an early warning of risk or opportunity. There is no universal formula, and simpler is usually better. A good health score includes:

  • Outcome measures: is the customer achieving what they bought? For Brindlepath, the ownership rate and follow-up rate at each site.
  • Adoption measures: are the expected users active? Is usage growing or falling?
  • Relationship signals: is there an engaged executive sponsor? Has the champion left?
  • Support signals: are there unresolved issues or a rising trend in tickets?
  • Commercial signals: are invoices paid on time? Has the customer asked about price or contract changes?

Weight outcome and adoption signals most heavily. Relationship signals matter, but a friendly contact can hide a failing deployment, as Tomás found at Ambermoor. Review health scores regularly and, more important, act on them: each at-risk customer should have an owner and a plan.

Turning feedback into product

Customer success teams hear more from customers than anyone else in the company. That knowledge belongs in the product.

Create a regular channel. Brindlepath’s customer success managers met the product trios every two weeks to share patterns: what customers struggled with, what they asked for, where they found workarounds.

Bring evidence, not just requests. “Three customers asked for bulk reassignment” is useful. “At three customers, navigators spend about 20 minutes each Monday reassigning weekend discharges one by one” is far more useful, because it describes the problem.

Close the loop. When customer feedback shapes the product, tell the customers who raised it. Few things build loyalty faster than seeing your suggestion in a release note.

Advocacy

Satisfied customers are your most credible marketing. In business software, and especially in healthcare, where buyers trust their peers far more than vendors, a reference call from a respected customer can decide a deal.

Build advocacy deliberately:

  • Help customers tell their story, in case studies, conference talks and peer conversations, with their outcomes and in their words.
  • Create a customer community, such as user groups or an advisory board, where customers learn from each other and from you.
  • Respect your advocates’ time. Do not overuse a small group of references. Reward them with early access, influence on the roadmap and recognition.
  • Get permission and stay accurate. Any claim about a customer’s results should be approved by the customer and supported by data.

Brindlepath in practice: the quarterly business review

Brindlepath’s customer success team rebuilt its quarterly business reviews around one principle: the customer’s outcomes come first, the product second.

Each review followed the same structure and lasted under an hour. It opened with the customer’s own goals, restated from the start of the relationship: for Ambermoor, reducing missed follow-ups and avoidable readmissions across its hospitals. Then came the outcome measures, trended over the quarter and the year, by hospital: the ownership rate, missed first follow-ups and the estimate of avoided readmissions from the outcome report. Then adoption: active navigators by site, with any site falling behind named openly and a plan to help. Then what the customer had told Brindlepath, and what Brindlepath had done about it. Only then the roadmap: what was coming that would help this customer specifically, and what the product team wanted to learn from them. The review closed with agreed next steps, each with an owner on both sides.

Two details made the difference. Tomás and his colleagues sent the outcome data to the customer’s champion a week ahead, so there were no surprises in front of executives. And they always invited the executive sponsor, not just the day-to-day users. If the sponsor could not attend, they rescheduled. A review without the person who decides on renewal is a status meeting.

Over two years, the reviews became one of the most valued parts of the relationship. Several customers began using the same outcome slides in their own board meetings, which was the clearest possible sign that Brindlepath had made its value visible.

Onboarding, redesigned

Before the 90-day finding in Chapter 10, Brindlepath’s onboarding was a sequence of technical steps: contract signed, integration built, users trained, live. Time to first value averaged more than five months, mostly spent waiting on integration work and approvals.

The redesign reorganized onboarding around first value. Integration moved onto the standard connector, which cut the technical work from months to weeks. One hospital and one navigator team went live first, rather than the whole health system at once. The customer’s navigator manager and Brindlepath’s onboarding lead shared a written plan with dates and a single goal: 80 percent ownership within 90 days of go-live at the first hospital. Training became short, role-specific sessions in the navigators’ own environment, followed by a check-in after the first week.

Average time to first value fell to under three months, and the share of new customers reaching 80 percent within 90 days rose sharply. Expansion to the remaining hospitals in each system began sooner, because the first hospital’s results made the case internally.

Common mistakes

Mistaking friendliness for health. A warm relationship with one contact can hide a failing deployment. Watch outcomes and usage, not just sentiment.

Ignoring onboarding. Customers who struggle through a long implementation often never fully recover their enthusiasm, whatever you do later.

Measuring support, not success. Ticket resolution time matters, but it does not tell you whether customers are achieving what they bought.

Treating renewal as a sales event. If value has not been shown all year, a renewal meeting is too late to start.

Burning out your advocates. The same three references asked for every deal soon stop answering. Grow your advocate community and reward the people in it.

Keeping customer knowledge in customer success. Patterns that customer success managers see every week belong in product decisions. Without a regular channel, they stay in their heads.

Try this

Pick your five largest customers. For each, write down their outcome measure, its trend over the last quarter, the number of active users by site, the name of their executive sponsor and the date of your last conversation with that sponsor. Mark any customer where the outcome or usage is falling, or where you are unsure the sponsor is still in place. Each marked customer gets an owner and a plan this week, before the renewal conversation makes the decision for you.

How AI changes this

AI can watch every account. An AI assistant can monitor usage, support tickets, emails and meeting notes across all customers and flag the kind of decline Tomás found at Ambermoor, without waiting for a quarterly review. It can draft the account summary before every call. Treat its alerts as prompts for a human conversation, not as conclusions.

AI can deliver help at the moment of need. In-product assistants that answer questions using your help content, guide users through tasks and explain what changed in a release can shorten onboarding and reduce support load. Make sure they draw only on accurate, current content, and hand off to a person when they cannot help.

AI can scale customer success. With AI handling research, preparation and routine follow-up, a customer success manager can serve more accounts with more attention, rather than less. The relationship itself, the trust built through honest conversations, stays human.

AI features need their own success plan. Customers adopting AI features often need more guidance, not less: what the feature is good at, where to double-check it, and how to give feedback when it is wrong. Build this into onboarding.
