chapters.title: Partnerships and Ecosystems
chapters.epigraph:
“If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

— proverb
chapters.html:
Two partnerships

In the same year, Brindlepath signed two partnerships that looked equally promising on paper.

The first was with a large consulting firm that advised health systems on care transitions. The firm’s partners loved Brindlepath’s product and agreed to recommend it to their clients. A press release went out. A joint webinar drew a big audience. Twelve months later, the partnership had produced one qualified lead. The consultants were paid for advice, not software, and recommending Brindlepath did nothing for their own targets.

The second was with a regional home-health company that cared for many of the patients Brindlepath’s customers discharged. It began as a modest technical integration: when a navigator assigned a patient to home health, the referral flowed directly into the home-health company’s system, with the discharge summary attached, instead of by fax. Within a year, the home-health company was asking its own hospital partners to adopt Brindlepath, because the integration cut its intake time in half. Three new customers came through that channel.

The difference was not enthusiasm. Both partners were enthusiastic. The difference was that the second partnership created value for both companies, every day, in the normal course of their work. The first depended on goodwill.

Why partner at all

Partnerships extend what a product can do and where it can reach, without building everything yourself. They are worth pursuing when they do at least one of four things:

  1. Complete the product. A partner fills a capability gap your customers need but that is not your core, such as Brindlepath’s integration with a scheduling partner when it retired its own scheduling product in Chapter 7.
  2. Extend reach. A partner gives you access to customers, channels or markets you could not reach efficiently alone.
  3. Strengthen the outcome. A partner sits elsewhere in the customer’s workflow, so connecting to them makes the end result better, as with the home-health integration.
  4. Accelerate innovation. A partner brings technology, data or expertise that lets you build something new faster, such as an AI model provider or a research institution.

Partnerships that do none of these are usually press releases.

Types of partnerships

Partnerships come in several forms, each with different economics and demands.

Technology and integration partners connect products so data and workflows flow between them: record systems, home-health and post-acute providers, identity providers, analytics platforms. They are the most common and often the most valuable, because they make the product more useful every day.

Platform and marketplace partners distribute your product through their ecosystem: an app marketplace attached to a record system, a cloud provider’s marketplace, or a larger vendor’s catalog. They can extend reach dramatically, at the cost of fees, rules and some dependence on the platform owner.

Channel and reseller partners sell your product, often bundled with their own services. They work best when selling your product helps them meet their own goals.

Services and implementation partners help customers deploy and get value from your product. For complex products, they can make implementation scalable.

Strategic and co-development partners build something new together, sharing investment, risk and rewards. They require the most trust and governance.

Choosing the right partners

Partnerships take real time and attention from small teams, so be selective. Before committing, assess each candidate on a few dimensions:

  • Mutual value: what does each side gain, concretely and measurably? If you cannot write down the partner’s gain in one sentence, the partnership will drift.
  • Customer overlap: do you serve the same customers, so that working together helps them?
  • Workflow fit: does the partnership connect naturally to how customers already work?
  • Incentive alignment: does working with you help the partner’s people hit their own targets?
  • Capability and commitment: does the partner have the people, technology and executive sponsorship to follow through?
  • Risk: data sharing, reputation, dependency, competition and regulatory exposure.

The consulting firm in the opening story scored well on customer overlap and poorly on incentive alignment. The home-health company scored well on almost everything, especially workflow fit.

Building the partnership

Once you choose a partner, treat the partnership like a product.

Agree on shared goals and measures. Referrals made, integrations live, patients transferred, time saved, joint revenue. Write them down and review them together.

Start small and prove value. Begin with a pilot: one integration, one region, one shared customer. Expand when it works.

Name owners on both sides. Every partnership needs a person on each side who is accountable for its success and has the authority to make decisions.

Make it easy to work together. Clear technical documentation, a sandbox for testing, simple commercial terms and a regular meeting rhythm.

Get the agreements right. In healthcare, any partnership that involves patient data needs the right data agreements, including business associate agreements where appropriate, as Chapter 11 described. Agree on data use, security, liability, intellectual property and how the partnership can end.

Building an ecosystem

As a product grows, its partnerships can become an ecosystem: a network of partners, customers and developers who build on and around the product. Ecosystems create value that no single company could: more integrations, more use cases, more reasons for customers to stay.

Ecosystems usually grow from a few foundations:

  • Open, well-documented interfaces that partners can build on without lengthy negotiation, using industry standards where they exist, such as HL7 FHIR in healthcare.
  • A partner program with clear tiers, benefits and requirements.
  • A marketplace or directory where customers can find partner integrations.
  • Shared success stories that show customers and prospective partners what is possible.

Brindlepath’s ecosystem began with three integrations and grew to more than twenty in three years: home-health and post-acute providers, transportation services, community organizations that helped patients with food and housing, and analytics partners. Each integration made the core product more valuable to every customer.

Navigating partnership challenges

Even good partnerships hit trouble. The most common problems are predictable.

Misaligned incentives. Priorities shift and the partnership stops serving one side. Review mutual value regularly, not just at signing.

Competing priorities. The partnership is your top priority and the partner’s tenth. Executive sponsorship on both sides helps; so does making the partnership part of each side’s measured goals.

Integration decay. Partners change their systems and integrations break. Monitor every integration, with alerts when data stops flowing, and agree on how changes will be communicated.

Becoming a competitor. A partner may build what you offer, or you may build what they offer. Discuss the boundaries openly and early, and plan for the possibility.

Dependence on a platform. If a large share of your business flows through one platform or marketplace, its rule changes can hurt you badly. Diversify where you can.

Ending well. Some partnerships should end. Plan how customers will be supported, how data will be handled and how integrations will be retired, as Chapter 7 described for products.

Brindlepath in practice: from referral to ecosystem

The home-health integration described at the start of the chapter grew into Brindlepath’s partner program over two years, and the way it grew is instructive.

It began with one integration, built to solve one shared problem: referrals sent by fax lost information and took days. The first version did one thing: when a navigator selected home health for a patient, the referral, with the discharge summary and medication list, appeared in the home-health company’s intake system within minutes. Both companies agreed on two measures, the time from referral to first home visit and the share of referrals that needed a follow-up phone call for missing information, and reviewed them monthly.

The results were strong enough that the home-health company started recommending Brindlepath to the hospitals it worked with, and other post-acute providers began asking for the same integration. Rather than build each one from scratch, Brindlepath turned the work into a standard referral interface based on HL7 FHIR, published its documentation, and created a simple partner program with two tiers: integrated partners, who had built and tested the interface, and strategic partners, who also shared measures and planning with Brindlepath.

The program grew to more than twenty partners: home-health agencies, skilled nursing facilities, transportation services and community organizations that helped patients with food and housing. Each partner integration was monitored, with alerts when referrals stopped flowing, and each had a named owner at Brindlepath.

Two partnerships ended along the way. One partner was acquired by a company that built a competing product; Brindlepath gave customers six months’ notice and helped them move referrals to other providers. Another never produced meaningful referral volume and was retired by mutual agreement. Ending partnerships well, as Chapter 15 recommends, kept the program’s reputation intact.

Common mistakes

Partnering for the press release. Announcements are easy. Partnerships that change nothing in either company’s daily work quietly fade.

Ignoring the partner’s incentives. If working with you does not help your partner’s people hit their targets, enthusiasm will not survive the next quarter.

Too many partners, too soon. Each partnership needs attention. A small company with twenty partners usually has twenty shallow ones.

No owner on either side. Partnerships without a named, accountable person on each side drift as soon as the first sponsor moves on.

Integrations without monitoring. A partner changes an interface, data stops flowing, and nobody notices until customers complain.

Becoming dependent on one platform. When a large share of revenue flows through one marketplace or platform, its rule changes become your crisis.

Try this

List your current and candidate partners. For each, write one sentence on what you gain and one on what they gain, then score them from one to five on customer overlap, workflow fit, incentive alignment and commitment. Any partnership where you cannot write the partner’s sentence, or that scores low on incentive alignment, deserves a frank conversation or a graceful exit. For your strongest partnership, agree on two shared measures and a date to review them together.

How AI changes this

AI model providers are a new kind of critical partner. Many products now depend on third-party AI models. That partnership carries the same questions as any other, mutual value, risk and dependency, plus new ones: how the provider handles your customers’ data, whether it trains on it, how model changes will affect your product’s quality, and what happens if prices change or a model is retired. Treat model providers as strategic partners, and design your product so you can switch providers if you must.

Integrations get easier, and more important. AI tools can help generate integration code and map data between systems, lowering the cost of new integrations. At the same time, AI features are only as good as the data they can reach, so integrations that bring in more context become more valuable.

AI agents will act across partner boundaries. As customers adopt AI agents that work across several systems, partnerships will increasingly be about how agents from different vendors can safely work together: what data they can exchange, what actions they can take, and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Emerging standards, such as protocols for connecting AI assistants to tools and data, are worth watching.

Partnership management benefits from AI too. Assistants can monitor partner integrations, summarize partner performance before reviews and spot co-selling opportunities across shared customers.

chapters.epigraph:
“Organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations.”

— Melvin Conway
chapters.html:
Twelve customers, then sixty

When Maya joined Brindlepath, it had twelve customers. Three years later, it had sixty. Almost nothing that worked at twelve worked at sixty without change.

At twelve customers, each implementation was a small craft project: an engineer spent weeks on each customer’s record integration, and the product had grown dozens of customer-specific settings, some of which nobody remembered the purpose of. At sixty, that approach would have needed a hundred engineers just for implementations. At twelve, Maya knew every customer’s chief nursing officer by name. At sixty, she could not. At twelve, two product teams coordinated over lunch. At sixty, seven teams needed a planning rhythm, shared standards and clear ownership, or they would trip over each other every week.

Scaling is not just doing more of the same. It is changing how the product and the company work, so that growth makes things better instead of breaking them.

Configure, don’t customize

The single most important product decision in scaling business software is how you handle the differences between customers. Every customer believes its workflow is unique. Some differences are real; many are habits. How you respond shapes your margins, your speed and your product’s quality.

At one end, every customer uses the same product in the same way. At the other, every customer has its own code. Healthy products sit near the left: one product, shared by all, with configuration, settings that customers or your team can change without engineering work, for the differences that genuinely matter, and extension points, such as open interfaces, where customers or partners can build what is unique to them.

Customization, building special code for one customer, feels like good service. It wins the deal in front of you. It also creates code that must be maintained, tested, secured and upgraded for that one customer forever, which is why Chapter 6’s three smallest customers were losing money. Brindlepath adopted a simple rule: a request for something customer-specific is first examined as a potential configuration available to everyone; if it cannot be, it goes to a partner or a services engagement, not into the core product.

Scaling the technology

Product leaders do not need to design architectures, but they do need to understand the trade-offs, because scaling problems show up as product problems: slow screens, outages, failed integrations, delayed features.

Multi-tenancy. Most SaaS products serve many customers from shared infrastructure, with each customer’s data kept strictly separate. It is far more efficient than running separate copies, and it requires careful design to make sure no customer can ever see another’s data.

Standard integrations. Replace one-off integrations with a standard connector, configured per customer. Brindlepath’s record connector, from Chapter 7, cut the time to integrate a new hospital from months to weeks.

Reliability targets. As customers depend on the product, reliability becomes a feature. Many teams set service level objectives (SLOs), explicit targets for availability and speed, and track how much of their allowed unreliability, their error budget, they have used. When the budget runs low, the team shifts effort from features to reliability. This turns an argument into a rule.

Observability. At scale, you cannot rely on customers to tell you when something is wrong. Monitoring, logging and alerting should show problems before customers notice them, especially for integrations, where a silent failure can mean patients missing from the queue.

Performance and cost. As usage grows, so do infrastructure and AI costs. Track cost per customer, as Chapter 6 recommended, and treat sudden increases as bugs.

Balancing quality with growth

Growth puts pressure on quality from every direction: more customers, more features, more engineers, more code. Without deliberate effort, quality erodes slowly and then all at once.

A few practices protect it:

  • Protect the capacity allocation from Chapter 5. Reliability, security and technical debt get their share every quarter, especially when growth is fastest.
  • Automate testing and release, so quality checks scale with the team rather than depending on heroics.
  • Use feature flags and staged rollouts to limit the impact of any single change.
  • Watch quality measures alongside growth measures: incident counts, error budgets, support tickets per customer, time to resolve.
  • Do blameless reviews after every significant incident, and fix the system, not just the symptom.

Compliance at scale

Compliance obligations grow with the business. New customers bring new security reviews. New states and countries bring new privacy laws. Larger customers ask for independent certifications. AI features bring new regulations.

Scale compliance the way you scale everything else: make it systematic.

  • Invest in certifications before you need them. A SOC 2 report or HITRUST certification takes months. Start before the big deal that requires it.
  • Build compliance into the platform. Audit logging, access controls, data retention and regional data storage built once, used everywhere.
  • Maintain the trust package from Chapter 11 as a living product.
  • Track regulatory change. Assign someone to watch the regulations that affect you and translate changes into product requirements early.

Expanding market reach

Growth eventually requires reaching beyond the first market. There are a few classic paths, each with its own risks.

Deeper in the same customers. More users, sites and modules within existing customers. Usually the cheapest growth, built on the customer success work in Chapter 14.

More customers in the same segment. Repeating what works with similar customers. Depends on a repeatable sales and implementation process.

Adjacent segments. New types of customers with similar problems. For Brindlepath, that meant large physician groups and health plans, which also needed to coordinate care after hospital discharges. Adjacent segments often need different buyers, messages and features, so treat each as a new product-market fit question, using the discovery methods in Chapters 2 and 3.

New geographies. New countries bring new regulations, languages, payment systems and buying habits. In healthcare, they also bring entirely different health systems. International expansion is rarely a matter of translation.

Expand one direction at a time, and only when the core is strong. A company that expands while its core product is still struggling usually ends up with two struggling products.

Scaling the organization

Melvin Conway’s observation at the top of this chapter has become known as Conway’s law: the structure of a system tends to mirror the communication structure of the organization that builds it. If three teams must coordinate to change one workflow, the product will show the seams.

The practical lesson is to design teams around the product you want. Brindlepath reorganized at about forty engineers from teams organized by technology layer to teams organized around customer journeys: the navigator’s day, discharge and integration, outcomes and reporting, and the patient’s experience, with a platform team providing shared services. Each journey team could deliver most changes on its own.

As the organization grows, the product leader’s job changes too:

  • From doing to enabling. Less time on individual features, more on strategy, hiring, coaching and the system that teams work within.
  • From conversations to written communication. Strategy pages, decision logs and product briefs replace hallway agreements.
  • From one roadmap to many. Each team owns its roadmap within a shared strategy and portfolio view.
  • From knowing every customer to knowing the patterns. Customer advisory boards, research programs and data replace personal relationships with every account, though product leaders should still talk to customers every week.

Brindlepath in practice: the configuration rule

When Brindlepath adopted its configuration rule, the product had accumulated 47 customer-specific code paths, settings and integrations over its first years. Dev Raman’s team estimated that maintaining them consumed close to a quarter of engineering capacity, mostly in testing and upgrades.

The team sorted them into three groups. Nineteen could become configuration available to every customer: for example, a customer-specific risk threshold became a setting any hospital could adjust, with sensible defaults. Fourteen belonged with partners or services: custom reports, for instance, moved to the outcomes module’s export and a reporting partner. And fourteen could simply be retired, because the customers who had asked for them no longer used them, or had never used them at all.

The migration took most of a year, done customer by customer, with notice and support. Some conversations were difficult; one customer had built a workflow around a special integration and needed months of help to move. But by the end, the share of engineering capacity spent on customer-specific maintenance had fallen to a small fraction of its former level, and the time to onboard a new customer had dropped sharply.

The rule also changed sales conversations. Instead of promising custom work, sellers could show prospects the configuration options available to every customer, the partner ecosystem for specialized needs, and the product’s open interfaces. Prospects who needed something truly unique were pointed to services or partners. A few deals were lost. Many more were won faster, and every customer benefited from a product that improved for all of them at once.

Common mistakes

Saying yes to custom work to win deals. Each custom request looks small. Together they become the maintenance burden that slows every release and erodes your margins.

Scaling a product that has not found fit. More sales and marketing on top of weak retention accelerates churn, not growth.

Letting reliability become an afterthought. As customers depend on you, outages cost more. Service level objectives and error budgets turn reliability into a managed commitment.

Expanding in every direction at once. New segments, new geographies and new products together stretch a growing company past breaking point.

Ignoring Conway’s law. Teams organized by technology layer produce products whose seams show to customers.

Keeping early-stage habits too long. Practices that worked with two teams, such as decisions in the hallway and a roadmap in one person’s head, break quietly at seven.

Try this

Make a list of every customer-specific setting, integration and code path in your product. For each, ask whether it could become a configuration available to every customer, whether it belongs with a partner, or whether it should be retired. Estimate the engineering time each one costs per year. Then pick the three most expensive and put a plan for each on the roadmap. Most teams find that a handful of special cases consume a surprising share of their capacity.

How AI changes this

AI changes the economics of scale. AI tools can automate parts of implementation, support, testing and documentation, reducing the people needed per customer. Companies can serve more customers with smaller teams than ever before. That is an opportunity to grow efficiently, but only if the core product is standardized enough for automation to work. AI does not rescue a product built on customization.

AI costs scale with usage. Unlike most software costs, AI inference costs grow with every request. At scale, small inefficiencies become large bills. Engineering for AI cost, by using smaller models where they are good enough, caching results and limiting unnecessary calls, becomes a real discipline.

AI governance must scale too. When many teams build AI features, they need shared standards: approved models and providers, evaluation requirements, safety reviews and monitoring. Chapter 17 describes the practices; scaling means making them part of the platform rather than leaving each team to invent its own.

AI can help leaders see the whole system. Summaries of incidents, customer feedback, delivery measures and roadmap progress across many teams help a product leader spot patterns that would otherwise take weeks to assemble. The judgment about what to do remains human.

chapters.html:
The demo that was almost perfect

Brindlepath’s Horizon 3 team, introduced in Chapter 7, had a bold idea: an AI agent that would read a high-risk patient’s discharge summary, medication list and recent notes, then draft a post-discharge plan for the navigator, covering who to call, what to ask, which follow-up appointments were needed and which warning signs to watch for. If it worked, a navigator could prepare for a call in two minutes instead of fifteen.

The first demo, to the leadership team, was stunning. The agent produced clear, well-organized plans in seconds. The CEO wanted to announce it at the industry’s biggest conference, six weeks away.

Maya asked for one thing first: an evaluation. The team assembled 300 real, anonymized discharge summaries and asked two experienced nurses to review the agent’s plans against the source documents. The plans were good, most of the time. But roughly one plan in thirty contained something that was not in the record: a medication the patient was not taking, or a follow-up appointment that had never been ordered. Every one of those errors was written as confidently as everything else.

In a demo, one error in thirty is invisible. In a product used for thousands of patients a month, it is dozens of dangerous mistakes every week.

The team did not abandon the idea. They changed it. The agent now cited the source line for every statement, flagged anything it could not find in the record, and presented its plan as a draft the navigator reviewed and confirmed, never as an instruction. They built an evaluation set that ran before every change, and monitored errors in production. They launched four months later, with one customer, and expanded as the evidence came in.

This chapter is about building AI products that survive contact with reality, and about leading teams in which AI agents do real work.

Where organizations are

AI adoption has moved fast. In McKinsey’s 2025 global survey, 88 percent of respondents said their organizations used AI in at least one business function, and 62 percent said they were at least experimenting with AI agents. Far fewer had scaled them: 23 percent reported scaling an agentic AI system somewhere in their enterprise, and in no single business function did more than 10 percent report scaled use of agents.1

The gap between experimenting and scaling is where product leadership matters most. The technology to build an impressive demo is widely available. The discipline to build something reliable, safe, affordable and genuinely useful is not.

When AI is the right tool

AI is not the answer to every problem, and using it where it does not fit creates cost and risk for no benefit. Before building an AI feature, ask what kind of problem it is.

AI tends to fit well when:

  • the work involves understanding or producing language, images or other unstructured content;
  • inputs vary widely and cannot be handled by simple rules;
  • a good draft saves significant time, even if a person reviews it;
  • some errors are acceptable, or can be caught by review;
  • there is enough data, or enough examples, to evaluate quality.

AI tends to fit poorly when:

  • the answer must be exactly right every time and can be computed with rules;
  • the stakes of an undetected error are severe and there is no practical review step;
  • the task is simple enough that ordinary software does it cheaply and reliably;
  • you cannot measure whether the output is good.

Brindlepath’s discharge-plan agent was a good fit for drafting, because summaries were long and varied and a draft saved real time, and a poor fit for acting alone, because an undetected error could harm a patient. The product design followed from that distinction.

How much should AI do on its own?

The most important design decision for an AI feature is its level of autonomy: how much it does without a person’s involvement. A useful way to think about it is as a ladder.

  1. Assist. AI answers questions or retrieves information when a person asks. The person decides what to do with it.
  2. Suggest. AI proposes a draft or recommendation; a person reviews, edits and accepts or rejects it.
  3. Act with approval. AI prepares an action, such as sending a message or updating a record, and a person approves it before it happens.
  4. Act within limits. AI acts on its own within defined boundaries, with monitoring and the ability for people to review and reverse.
  5. Act autonomously. AI acts on its own across a broad scope. Rarely appropriate in high-stakes domains today.

Match the step to the consequences of being wrong. Drafting a patient-education handout might reasonably sit at suggest. Updating the ownership of a patient in the queue might sit at act with approval. Changing a medication should not sit anywhere on this ladder without a clinician’s decision. Start lower than you think you need to, measure, and climb only when the evidence supports it.

Designing AI experiences people can trust

AI features behave differently from traditional software. They are probabilistic: the same input can produce different outputs, and the output is sometimes wrong in ways that look right. Good AI design makes those properties visible and manageable.

Show the sources. Let people see where an answer came from. Brindlepath’s agent cites the line in the discharge summary behind every statement, so a navigator can verify it with one click.

Signal uncertainty. Flag what the AI could not find or is unsure about, instead of letting it guess confidently.

Make correction easy. Editing a draft should be faster than writing from scratch. If it is not, people will stop using the feature.

Keep people in control. Make it clear what the AI has done and what it will do next, and let people stop, undo or override it.

Label AI output. People should always know when content was produced by AI.

Capture feedback. Every acceptance, edit and rejection is a signal about quality. Collect it, with appropriate privacy protections, and use it to improve.

Design for the reviewer’s time. As Chapter 12 noted, AI that saves the author’s time but costs the reviewer more is not a gain. Measure total time, not just generation time.

Evaluation: the discipline that separates demos from products

Traditional software is tested with expected outputs: given this input, the result must be exactly that. AI features need evaluation: systematic measurement of output quality across many realistic examples, against criteria people agree on.

A practical evaluation program has five parts.

1. An evaluation set. A collection of realistic inputs, including hard and unusual cases, ideally drawn from real data with sensitive details removed. Brindlepath’s started with 300 discharge summaries and grew to over 1,000, deliberately including the messiest records the team could find.

2. Clear criteria. What does good look like? For the discharge plan: every statement supported by the record; no missing high-risk medications; correct follow-up appointments; plain language. Criteria should be specific enough that two reviewers agree.

3. Scoring. Expert human review is the gold standard, especially in clinical settings. Automated checks, and AI models used as graders under careful supervision, can scale evaluation, but should be calibrated regularly against human judgment.

4. Thresholds. Decide in advance what quality is good enough to launch, and what change in quality blocks a release. For Brindlepath, any unsupported clinical statement in the evaluation set blocked a release until it was understood.

5. Production monitoring. Track quality in real use: acceptance and edit rates, user-reported errors, sampled expert review, cost and speed. Real-world inputs drift over time, and model updates can change behavior. Feed problems you find in production back into the evaluation set.

Evaluation is not a one-time gate. It is the core quality process for any AI product, and it deserves the same investment as testing does for traditional software. A team that cannot measure its AI feature’s quality cannot improve it, and should not ship it.

Grounding AI in your data

General-purpose models know a great deal about the world and nothing about your customer. Most useful AI features combine a model with the right context: the customer’s records, documents, policies and history. A common approach, often called retrieval-augmented generation, finds the relevant information and provides it to the model with each request, instructing it to answer from that information.

Grounding has several benefits: answers reflect the customer’s actual situation, sources can be cited, and errors are easier to detect. It also means your data quality, integrations and permissions become part of your AI quality. An agent that can see the wrong patient’s record, or none of the right ones, will produce the wrong answer however good the model is. The integration work in Chapters 15 and 16 is AI work too.

Cost, speed and model choice

Every AI request has a cost and a delay. At small scale, they are easy to ignore. At scale, they shape the product and its margins, as Chapter 6 warned.

  • Use the smallest model that meets the quality bar. Larger models are often more capable and more expensive. Many tasks are handled well by smaller, faster, cheaper models.
  • Don’t call a model when you don’t need to. Cache results, avoid regenerating unchanged content, and use ordinary code for anything deterministic.
  • Design for latency. Show progress, stream results, or run work in the background so people are not left waiting.
  • Keep the option to switch. Model providers change prices, capabilities and terms. An architecture that can swap models, with an evaluation set to confirm quality after a switch, protects you, as Chapter 15 recommended.

Safety, security and responsibility

AI features introduce risks that product leaders must own, building on Chapter 11.

Harmful errors. In domains like healthcare, wrong outputs can hurt people. Keep humans in the loop for consequential decisions, evaluate rigorously, and monitor in production.

Bias and fairness. Models can perform worse for some groups of people than others. Evaluate quality across the groups your product serves, including by age, language and other relevant characteristics, and address gaps before launch.

Manipulation and misuse. AI systems can be tricked through their inputs, for example by instructions hidden in a document an agent reads. Limit what agents can access and do, treat external content as untrusted, and require approval for consequential actions.

Privacy. Know exactly what data reaches each model, where it is processed, whether it is retained, and whether it is used for training. Get the agreements in place before data flows.

Regulation. Requirements are evolving: medical device rules for clinical AI, the EU AI Act’s obligations for high-risk systems, state laws and sector guidance. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a practical structure for governing, mapping, measuring and managing AI risks.2 Involve legal and compliance partners early, as Chapter 11 recommended.

Leading teams that include AI agents

AI agents increasingly do real work inside product organizations: drafting research syntheses, triaging support tickets, monitoring dashboards, writing and reviewing code, preparing release notes. Treating them well is now part of leadership.

A practical way to think about it: manage an agent the way you would manage a new team member with specific, limited responsibilities.

  • Give it a job description. What exactly does it do, for whom, with what inputs, and what does good output look like?
  • Give it an owner. A named person is accountable for each agent’s instructions, permissions, quality and failures, as Chapter 8 recommended.
  • Limit its permissions. Grant access only to the data and actions its job requires. Review those permissions regularly.
  • Review its work. Sample its output, track its quality, and correct it. Agents do not improve by themselves; their owners improve them.
  • Make it visible. Everyone should know which work is done by agents, and how to raise a concern about it.
  • Keep humans accountable for decisions. Agents can gather, draft, recommend and, within limits, act. Accountability for outcomes, especially those affecting customers, money, safety or people, stays with people.

The product leader’s job is to design the system in which people and agents work together well: deciding which work suits agents, where human judgment must stay, and how quality is assured across both. That is the “orchestrator” role from Chapter 1, in practice.

From idea to AI product

Pulling it together, a practical path for building an AI product or feature looks like this:

  1. Start with the problem, using the discovery methods in Chapters 2 and 3, not with the technology.
  2. Check the fit: is AI the right tool, and what is the cost of an error?
  3. Choose the autonomy level based on the consequences of being wrong.
  4. Build the evaluation set early, before the feature, with experts defining good.
  5. Prototype quickly and measure against the evaluation set, not against a demo.
  6. Design the experience for trust: sources, uncertainty, easy correction, control.
  7. Pilot with a small group, monitor closely, and expand on evidence.
  8. Monitor quality, cost and safety in production, and feed what you learn back into evaluation.

Brindlepath’s discharge-plan drafts followed that path. In the story, navigators accepted about seven in ten plans with minor or no edits, preparation time per high-risk patient fell substantially, and the share of high-risk patients contacted within 24 hours rose at the pilot customer. Those results are part of the fictional example; your numbers will depend on your product and data. The method is what transfers.

Brindlepath in practice: the evaluation set

The evaluation set for the discharge-plan agent became one of the most valuable assets the company owned.

It began with 300 discharge summaries from two pilot customers, used with permission under the customers’ agreements, with names, dates and other identifying details removed. The team deliberately over-sampled hard cases: patients with long medication lists, summaries with contradictory information, handwritten notes scanned into the record, and patients transferred between hospitals.

Two experienced nurses wrote the quality criteria with the team. Every statement in a plan must be supported by the record. Every high-risk medication must be mentioned. Follow-up appointments must match what was ordered. Warning signs must be appropriate to the diagnosis. The language must be plain enough for a new navigator to act on. Each criterion was scored pass or fail, so that two reviewers would agree.

The nurses reviewed the first runs by hand. As the set grew, the team added automated checks, for example matching every medication in a plan against the medication list, and an AI-assisted grader for criteria that were harder to automate. The grader’s scores were compared each month against a sample reviewed by the nurses, and recalibrated when they drifted apart.

Every proposed change to the agent, whether a new instruction, a new model version or a new data source, ran against the full set before release. Twice, a change that looked better in a demo made the evaluation results worse, and was not released. Once, a model provider’s update changed behavior subtly; the evaluation caught it before any customer saw it.

Production monitoring fed the set. Every plan a navigator flagged as wrong was reviewed, and the most instructive cases, with details removed, were added to the evaluation set. After a year it held over 1,000 cases and reflected the real variety of the work far better than any test the team could have invented.

Common mistakes

Starting with the model instead of the problem. “We should use AI” is not a product idea. A validated customer problem is where every AI feature should begin.

Judging quality by the demo. Demos show the best case. Evaluation across hundreds of realistic examples shows what customers will actually experience.

Too much autonomy, too soon. Letting AI act on its own before the evidence supports it turns occasional errors into customer incidents.

Hiding the AI. Unlabeled AI output, without sources, makes errors harder to catch and erodes trust when they are found.

Ignoring cost until the invoice arrives. AI costs scale with use. A feature that is affordable in a pilot can be ruinous at scale.

Agents without owners. An AI agent with broad permissions and nobody accountable for it is an incident waiting to happen.

Try this

Pick one AI feature you have built, or are considering. Write its evaluation plan using the template in the Appendix: purpose, autonomy level, cost of an error, evaluation set, criteria, thresholds, fairness checks, monitoring and owner. If you cannot fill in the evaluation set and the criteria, stop and build them before you write another line of the feature. Then write a job description, from the Appendix template, for one AI agent your team uses, and check that its permissions match it.

“Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.”

— Dwight D. Eisenhower
chapters.html:
Three years later

Three years after her first Monday on the train, Maya Smith sat in the same quarterly business review with Ambermoor Health that had been on her overnight digest that first morning. The meeting was different now.

Ambermoor’s chief nursing officer opened with her own numbers: the share of high-risk patients with a confirmed owner within 24 hours had held above 85 percent for a year across seven hospitals. Missed first follow-ups had fallen. The finance team had used Brindlepath’s outcome report to show the board what avoided readmissions were worth. The navigators, she said, no longer spent their mornings on the phone trying to find out who owned whom.

Then she asked about the future. Could the discharge-plan drafts cover more patients? Could specialist offices see the handoff too? Could Brindlepath help with the health plan’s members as well as the hospital’s patients?

None of those questions was answered by a single feature, a single framework or a single chapter of this book. Each one touched the problem worth solving, the strategy and positioning, the numbers, the team, trust, customers, partnerships and AI. That is the nature of product leadership: the pieces only work when they work together.

This last chapter pulls the playbook into one picture, offers a practical rhythm for running it, and closes with some thoughts about the job.

One system, not seventeen chapters

Each chapter of this book covers one part of the work. In practice, they form a single system, where decisions in one area shape every other.

Some of the connections Brindlepath lived through:

  • The problem shapes the business. Choosing post-discharge ownership over scheduling (Chapter 2) made a value-based price possible (Chapter 6), because the value was measurable in avoided readmissions.
  • Strategy shapes the team. The not-doing list (Chapter 4) freed a third of engineering capacity, which funded the reliability work (Chapter 5) and the integration platform (Chapter 7).
  • Economics shape the product. Discovering that custom integrations made small customers unprofitable (Chapter 6) led to the standard connector (Chapter 16), which made partnerships possible (Chapter 15).
  • Trust opens markets. Treating security and accessibility as product requirements (Chapter 11) shortened every sales cycle that followed (Chapter 13).
  • Customers close the loop. A customer success manager’s early warning (Chapter 14) revealed a data problem that became a product fix, and a renewal became an expansion.
  • AI raises the stakes on everything. The discharge-plan agent (Chapter 17) depended on the integrations, the evaluation discipline, the trust practices and the team habits built over the previous three years.

When you face a decision, ask which other parts of the system it touches. Most product mistakes come from optimizing one part while ignoring the rest.

The four pillars, revisited

Chapter 1 described four pillars of product leadership. Looking back, each runs through the whole playbook.

Market understanding is not a phase. It begins with problem discovery and continues through every customer conversation, field visit, cohort analysis and renewal.

Financial insight is not a budget exercise. It informs which problems to solve, how to price, what to build, how to scale and which partnerships to pursue.

Customer-centered innovation is not a design department. It is the habit of every team member who watches users work and measures whether the product actually helped.

Trust and responsibility is not a compliance review. It is built into every requirement, every release, every AI feature and every partnership.

A product leader strong in all four, and able to connect them, is rare and valuable. Most of us are stronger in some than others. Know your weakest pillar and work on it deliberately, or hire people who are strong where you are not.

An operating rhythm

Frameworks are only useful if they are used regularly. The following rhythm, adapted from what worked at Brindlepath and in teams I have led, puts the playbook into practice.

Weekly. Customer conversations for every product trio. Review of input metrics and health scores. Team planning and decision log updates. Thirty minutes of customer feedback review with customer success.

Monthly. Product review of outcomes against the roadmap. Review of AI feature quality and cost. Partner integration health check. A field visit for at least one trio.

Quarterly. Roadmap and capacity allocation review. Portfolio review with stage-appropriate measures. Business reviews with key customers. Launch reviews for anything released in the quarter. Retrospective on how the team is working.

Yearly. Strategy refresh: diagnosis, guiding policy, actions and the not-doing list. Vision check. Pricing and packaging review. Horizon allocation for the year ahead.

The rhythm matters more than the exact meetings. Without it, urgent work crowds out important work, and strategy becomes something you write once a year and forget.

Your first 90 days as a product leader

Many readers will use this book when starting a new product role. A practical plan for the first 90 days, drawn from Maya’s experience and my own:

Days 1 to 30: listen and learn.

  • Meet every member of the product, design and engineering teams one to one.
  • Talk to at least ten customers, including some who left or said no.
  • Spend time where the product is used, as Lena did in Chapter 12.
  • Learn the numbers: revenue, margin, retention, cost to serve, as in Chapter 6.
  • Read the existing strategy, roadmap and backlog, and the last year of decisions, if anyone wrote them down.
  • Change very little.

Days 31 to 60: diagnose and align.

  • Write your diagnosis: what is working, what is not, and the hardest problem the product faces.
  • Test it with the leadership team, the product team and a few trusted customers.
  • Identify one or two quick wins that demonstrate progress and build trust.
  • Clean up the backlog, as Maya did in Chapter 5.

Days 61 to 90: decide and communicate.

  • Write the one-page strategy, including the not-doing list.
  • Agree on the North Star and input metrics.
  • Rebuild the roadmap around outcomes.
  • Set the operating rhythm.
  • Tell the story, repeatedly.

Common mistakes

Optimizing one part of the system. A brilliant feature that the economics cannot support, or a strong strategy that the team cannot deliver, fails just as surely as a weak one.

Collecting frameworks. Frameworks help only when they are used regularly, by the whole team, to make real decisions. A rhythm matters more than a library.

Changing everything in the first month. New leaders who reorganize, rewrite the strategy and rebuild the roadmap before they understand the product lose the trust they need later.

Forgetting to look at the results. Plans are useful; results are what count. Build the habit of checking whether what you did made the difference you expected.

The job, honestly

Product leadership is a strange job. You are accountable for outcomes you cannot directly control. You have authority over very little and influence over almost everything. You are expected to be right about the future while knowing that much of what you believe is wrong. You spend your days choosing what not to do, and disappointing someone with almost every choice.

It is also one of the best jobs in business. You get to understand people’s problems deeply, assemble talented teams to solve them, and see the results in the lives of the people you serve. In healthcare, that can mean a patient who gets the call she needed, from a navigator who knew she was his, because a team made a hundred careful decisions about how that should work.

AI will keep changing how the work is done. Agents will take on more of the gathering, drafting, analyzing and monitoring. The tools in this book will evolve. But the core of the job, understanding people, choosing well, building trust and owning the outcome, will remain human for a long time. The best product leaders of the next decade will be the ones who use every tool available to do that core job better, and never confuse the tools with the job.

I hope this playbook helps you do it.
